div.head: FARM AND GARDEN,
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN,
FOOD INSPECTION.
Cheshire Farmers and a Cheese
Difficulty,

The proceedings of the Board of Agriculture and Fisheries (Intelligence Division) under the Sale of Food and Drugs Act, the Fertilisers and Feeding Stuffs Act, and various other Acts, for the year 1912 was issued on Monday. There were 2,135 samples taken during the year by officers of the Board of Customs and Excise at the ports of the United Kingdoin,which comprised 1,230 of butter, 295 of margarine, 49 of milk, 137 of condensed milk, 61 of cream, and 63 of cheese. Of the total, 28 samplus were reported against. The total number of samples taken in England and Wales under the Sale of Food and Drugs Acts increased from 103,221 in 1911 to 108,174 last year. The number of samples of milk taken in 1912 was 52,501, against 50,849 in 1911, and the number of samples of butter taken in 1912 was 21,721, against 20,887 in the previous year. The butter factories registered bad increased during the 3 ear from 203 to 211, of which 29 were in London, 61 in Wales, and 118 in the rest of England. "HALF-MEAT" CHEESE SOLD AS "CHESHIRE."

A complaint was received by the Board from an asscciation of Cheshire farmers that " half-meat cbeese was being sold as " Cheshire." In otder to ascertain the exact nature of the crrnplaint the Board arranged a meeting between certain members of the association and one of their cfficers. In the course of this meeting it transpircd.that their complaint was that "half-meat " cheese was sold in places nhich dealt almcst exclusively iii" Cheshire " cheese, or in circumstances cilculated to lead the purchaser to suppose that the cheese was " Cheshire." The methods by which this practice could be st pped were fully discussed, and it was arranged that the matter shculd be referred back to the association for further consideration. LOCAL FARMER'S LOSS.

A request for advice was received from a f amer near Wariington, who had 1, St within a fortnight of arrival, 28 out of 328 lambs sent by rail from Glen- finnan, Scotland, to Kenyon, near Warrington. The time occupied on the j ,urney, a distance f 331 miles, was thirty-three hours, and the lambs were without food or water for that period- hquiries by one of the inspectors of the Board (licked the fact that the consigner hd not made any request to the railway company to water or feed the suck, although they were conveyed during the latter part of August, when traffic on the lines concerned is heavy, and that the lambs had been overfed immediately after the journey.

div.head: FARM LABOURERS' STRIKE.
div.p: THE FARM LABOURERS' STRIKE.

The negotiations betn eert the S. uth-west Lanca- shire farmers and their men for the settlement of the strike have been Euspended by the refusal of the farmers to treat until the demand for union recogni- tion has been formally abandoned and the men advised to resume wok. The union has rejected this proposal.

div.head: ROYAL SHOW.
div.p: THE ROYAL SHOW.

The Royal Show at Bristol this week Las been favoured IT brilliant weather. The honorary director, Sir Gilbert Greenall, has, as usual, been diligent in his supervision, and in carrying out the wcrk he has been ably supported by Mr. Mellow, the secretary; Mr. Naylor, the surveyor ; and the staff. The exhibition, magnificently equipped within an expanse of 100 acres, was on a colossal scale, worthy of the best traditions of the Royal Show. The total number of entries was 11,308, and they included a display of no fewer than 5,652 implements. Five hundred and eighty-four horses were entered for prizes amounting to £3,591, and the cattle classed comprised 1,138 animals, amongst which 3:2,851 was divided. There were 736 sheep and 394 pigs, poultry entries numbered 1,436, and produce 685. The prize-money offered amounted to nearly £ll,OOO. A notable feature was the tuccess of the King's exhibits. His Majesty, who sent cattle from Windsor, and cattle, sheep, and p;gs from Sandi ingbam, gained no fewer than 30 awards. These it eluded the champion prize of £2O for a shorthorn heifer from Windsor, and a silver medal for Southdown ewes from Sandringham. At Sandringhatn the King is going in for the Berk- shire, the pig which, as everybody knows, supplies us with our Wiltshire hams and bacon. Ho has taken the first prize for a young boar. Sir Gilbert Greenall is now the principal breeder of the large whites, which are pat ticularly massive beasts The prize-winners included Lord Gerard and Sir Gilbert Oreenall.

Hackneys.—Pony stallion, foaled before 1910 : 1, Joshua Ball, Warrington, Southworth• Swell. Pony colt, filly or gelding: 2, Jcslitta Ball. Hunters—Novice five-year-olds: 2, G. P. Dewhurst, Northwicb, Delamere.

div.head: NEW BREEDS OF WHESTS.
div.p: NEW BREEDS OF WHESTS.

Messrs. Garton's Limited, the vell-known firm of farm plant breeders and seed experts of Warrington and Acton Grange, Cheshire, have a most interesting display of their new and regenerated breeds of farm plants at the Royal Agricultural Nociety's Show at Bristol this week. New and regenerated breeds of triad wheats are leading features on this stand, including exhibits of these from his Majesty King George's Royal Farms at, Windsor, and from the home farm of his Grace, the Duke of Westminster, Aldford, Chester, as well as from the home farms of Earl Beauchamp, Madresfield Court, Worcester, 'and the Earl of Coventry, Croome Court, Worcester. These wheats include the new and regenerated breeds of " Victor," " Squareheads Master" and " Browick," which have met with such remarkable successe s in the open trials conducted by the Yorkshire County Council at the University of Leeds, the Harper-Adams (Salop) Agricultural College, and other agricultural centres. On the home far' of the Earl of Rosebery, Dalmeny, Midlothian, one of these new breeds pro- duced the extraordinary yield of 80 bush' is per acre.

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.

PRUNING SCOTCH PosEs.—This is the best time to prune large, thickly-furnished bushes of these early and sweet roses. The pruning consists in cutting out the oldest of the shoots, so that younger ones, which are the more floriferous, may have ample space during the rest of the season, Young plants may be left till autumn rani then slightly pruned in a similar manner; but neither young nor old plants should be severely thinned, otherwise they will become straggly, and to enable them to regain their former stiffness a number of growths have to be cut back.—" The Garden." STAKING DAHLIAS. —lf not already staked and tied dahlias should be attended to at once. Those intended for exhibition should have the central growth pinched out, selecting four shoots horn the resulting breaks, and tying each to a stake, sloping them in an outward direction so as to admit as much light and air as possible to the centre of the plants. At present only sufficient water need be given to prevent the plants from flagging, but when coming into flower they should not be stinted in this respect.—" Th.e Garden.'

div.head: PROVISION FOR AGED GARDENERS.
div.p: PROVISION FOR AGED GARDENERS.

Now that our gardens are at the zenith of their beauty and interest, it is fitting that we spare a thought to those who have in the past, directly or iadirectly, given us many of the beautiful fruits and flowers that we now eniiy. At the annual festival dinner of the Gardeners' Royal Benevolent Institution, the hon. treasurer, Sir Harry J. Veitch, thew a vivid, but by no means imaginary picture of the destitution of many aged or infirm gardeners, or the widows of gardeners, for whose benefit the institution exists. In spite of increased subscriptions each year, there are still many thoroughly deserving candidates who cannot be put on the funds because sufficient money is not available. The plight of these aged or infirm gardeners has not been brought about through any fault of their own.—" Country Life."

div.head: SLUMP IN POLITICAL CLUBS.
div.p: SLUMP IN POLITICAL CLUBS.

Two prominent political clubs in St. Helens have been closed during the past week. The British Consti- tutional Labour party, a Tory organisation, which was mainly responsible for the actions brought against the miners' federation by which injunctions were obtained restraining the federation from ear-marking part or their funds for political work, carried on a club in Church-street for some years, but this has been closed and the premises vacated, it being understood that the club did not pay. Then the Socialist Club, also in Church-street, was sold up during the week. It is stated that differences between the I.L.P. Socialists, who have been very vigorous in propaganda work in the district, and the British Socialist party havb caused a great falling off in club membership, and it was decided to sell up the furniture and carry on the work on a smaller scale,

div.head: WOMEN'S QUESTIONS.
div.p: WOMEN'S QUESTIONS.
How Dress Adds to the Animation and Brightness of the Streets. OPEN-AIR DANCING. London streets owe much_ of their animation and

brightness in summer to the gay colours of the women's dresses, and the many hues of their flower-crowned hats. This display of colour never fails to strike the foreigner who visits the Metropolis during the season, or the traveller on his return from a lengthy sojourn in Continental cities. Parisiennes wear more sombre garb in the streets, and the toilettes to be seen at noon in Bond- street, any day in June or July, would in Paris he reserved for luncheon parties or for five o'clock. If women were less prodigal of colour, our streets would be even more sombre than they are, and it would considerably lessen their gloom and leaden greyness in winter if women chose bright colours for that season's suits, or even carried gaily coloured umbrellas in wet weather. Some years ago it was said that as r, nation we weie afraid of colour, but, if so we are certainly losing all fear of displaying it in summer t.rne. WOMEN OF TIIE BOURGEOISIE. The position of women in France and in Britain is quite different ; a Frenchwoman attains freedom from the control of her relations only when she marries. In many respects the status of the married woman is far better than in this country, although a greater number of wives among the middle classes go out to work if their husbands are not in busii ess for them- selves, in which care the wife is always the chief assistant, confidante, and adviser. The pc sition of the &Wish wife, who knows nothing of her husband's business affairs, is almost unknown among the French bourgeoisie. Nearly half the female populafon of France are wage-tarners, or cccupied in some trade or profession, and quite a third of the married women go era to work. At a popular Lycee for girls there are forty women professors, and at least the half are married women. Some are the wives of Government clerks with comparatively small salaries, but the women are the real bread-winners, and almost invari- ably they make excellent mothieis and housekeepers. The learned prole sons attract many FI end' women, and in Paris alone there are twenty-seven lady advo- cates or barristers. LHE FIRST LADY LAWYER. The honour of possessing the first fully qualified lady lawyer belongs to Italy, which has produced so many remaikable women. Among prominent women lawyers of to-day is Miss Clara Butt Martin, ef Toronto, who is the pioneer lady barrister of Canada. It was in a great measure due to her untiring efforts that women were admitted to the learned profession in Canada. Mrs. Belva Ann Lockwood, the first w, man to practise as a barrister in the United States, after a spirited controversy, was admitted to the Bar of the Supreme Court of Columbia, and has been actively engaged in law practice ever since. Miss Martin also is a popular member of the legal profession in Toronto, with a pra.stice many successful men might envy. OPEN-AIR DANCING. The French are said to be born under a dancing star, while in the more sedate country of Sweden dancing in the open-air is a national amusement, and there seems a probability that, thanks to the endeavours of the Guild of Morris dancers, the amuse- ment that was once a part of our national life may be restored, end dancing may again cccupy the position it held before the Reformation. Dancing in some of the London parks has already been added t ) the amusements of the Metropolis; and a request has been made to the London County Council by Mrs. Clare- mont, a rt sident of Hampstead for the assistance of a band to enable her, and other ladies interested in educational and social work, to organise a programme for Bank Holidays, on the celebrated Heath, in order to encourage graceful dancing, not only for the children, but among the grown-ups. Seeing that the children have been taught old English dances in the schools for some years past, there can be no objection to such dances being practised in the parks. Last year there was public dancing in the parks at Chiswick and Willesden, and the pastime has been resumed in Round way Park, where as many as two and three thousand people often congregate to watch the dancers. BATHING DRESSES. The range of materials wed for this season's bath- ing dress( s is astonishing. Taffetas, silk, sponge cloths, figured aid plain crepon, satins and silky alpacas,,are but a fevv of the fabrics that have been annexed by des;gners and dressmakers, and of this list the most popular are decidedly crepons and sponge cloths. Although navy serge still has some faithful admirers, it comes very low down on the list of fashionable goods used in this connection. With regard to styles anything that is worn for coats and f. ocks may be easily adopted, and those dresses intended for the parade at a smart Continental water- ing place have tunics that would not be out of place on an afternoon dress. But English women require dresses for the water, and the swimmer who means business demands a practical, and not too ornamental a costume, which, at the same time, can be quite pretty and becoming. Quite naturally the colour craze has influenced this depart- ment of attire, as well as every other, and many costumes are gorgeous in a blaze of vivid greens, blues, yellows and purples. Girls with fair skins look their best in all-black gowns, and for these taffetas or black satin, when of god quality, is one of the beet materials. Saxe blue crepon, with black satin deep collar, belt, and buttons, looks very well, with touches of pink embroidery. The cap should be black, with embroidered device in hoot to match that on the tunic.

DUTCH CAPS AND POKE BONNETS. Bathing-caps, like the costumes worn with them, have improved marvellously, and are as picturesque and becoming as they are diverse in shape, but as these do not preserve the hair from contact with the sea water, recourse must be had to the waterproof sponge bag affair that is hideous in the extreme, but still useful to wear underneath the dainty mob, turban, Dutch bonnet, or even poke bonnet, all of which, and many others too numerous to mention, are pressed into the service of bathers this year. A pretty cap has made its appearance that may be recommended for its utility and economy. It is made of thin water- proof coloured silk, and with the addition of a little pleated frill gives the necessary, artistic touch. NECK-WEAR. The ruffle that has come to us from the quaint siyles of the beginning of the last century is quite in harmony with this summer's dainty frocks. It is usually built of tulle or of spotted net,but occasionally from the same material as the dress, when that is composed of some flimsy fabric such as mousseline de- soie, soft silk, or chiffon and lace. The kerchief of tulle caught together with a rose or jewel looks picturesque,and may be depended upon to rejuvenate a last year's corsage. A distinct chaim is given to this dainty accessory when it is handmade, but of course it must be perfectly fresh and clean to gve a desirable finish to a simple dress. • How to Make

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
Can the Children See the King at Warrington?
The forti.igVtly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardiaus ells held at Dutton on Tuesday, Mr. Linaker jun., preticiing. THE CHILDREN'S HOME.

At a meeting of the Children's Home Committee it was decided that the present arrangements for the medical inspection of the children before entering the homes be continued for the time being ; that the atten- tion of the agent for the Aston estate be called to the fact that the wall across the girls' ground was in a dangerous state ; that the tender of Messrs. Merry- weather for the supply of fire buckets for £2 19s. be accepted. The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: CHILDREN AND THE KING'S VISIT.
div.p: THE CHILDREN AND THE KING'S VISIT.

The Superintendent asked the Board for permission to take the children to see the King at Warrington OD Monday, for a subscription of about £2, and permission from the tchool authorities for a holiday for the children. _

Mr. Lister-Kaye : Can we get them a pass? The Chairman : Can we get them sitting or standing room. He added that it was very nice to show the children n hat loyalty meant, but if they were going to get lost, it would he very unfortunte. Mr. Lister-Kaye: Unless you have a place allotted to you, I doubt whether they will have an opportunity of seeing the King and Queen. Ile did not believe they would be able to accommodate them anywhere, if they got to Warrington. The Chairman : Do the Guardians think it desirable that they should go? (Several Voices, "No.") Mr. Goddard (superintendent) : My idea was to arrange with the superintendent of the police. Mr. Woodward : Can Mr. Pilling say anything as a Warrington man ? _ _ _

Mr. Pilling: I don't think there is any possibility of them getting to see the King. Mr. C. E. Linaker : One does not like to damp this sort of thing. It would be nice if the children could be taken somewhere on the road where they will have the opportunity of seeing the King. It was decided that the Clerk write the Warrington Corporation to ascertain if it would be possible to arrange the p-sijon for the children. Mr. Lister-Kaye: You will have to get them on a 'bus, or you will not see them again.

div.head: PROPOSED MONTHLY MEETINGS.
div.p: PROPOSED MONTHLY MEETINGS.

Mr. Linaker (sent.) voiced the desire that the meet- ings of the Board should be held monthly instead of fortnightly. He moved that the Clerk be authorised to consider the matter, and get out a scheme whereby the House Committee could meet on the intermediate Tuesday. Mr. Lister-Kaye": Many District Councils only meet once per month. Mr. Linaker : The majority. The Chairman : We are Guardians at present, Mr. Rave. _ _
Linker : It is they who are the obstacles.
The Clerk promised to get out a scheme.

div.head: TAXI-CAB TRAGEDY.
div.p: TAXI-CAB TRAGEDY.
Warrington Chauffeur Exonerated
from Blame.

The tragic deaih of Walter Ditchfield (11), foreman pin maker, 10, River-road, who was knocked down by a, taxi-cab near Wilderspool Crossings, on Saturday night, was irquired into by Mr. S. l3righouse, County Corcner on Wednesday. Mr. T. S. Steel appeared for the relatives, Mr. Herbert Hatton (Messrs. Robert Davies and Co.) for Messrs. Greenell, Whitley and Co., the owners of the taxi-cab, and Mr. Chapman, of Manchester, for William Whitelegge, the chauffeur. The evidence showed that at 10.35 deceased and his wife were returning home from a picture palace, and the wife declared that deceased was perfectly sober. Ditchtleld called in the Ring O'Bells inn, his wife going home to prepare supper. On coming out he was crossing the roadway when he was knocked down by the taxi-cab and sustained a fractured skull. _ _

Mr. Henry Greensll, solicitor, who, along with his wife and daughter, was travelling in the taxi-cab, said the speed at which the vehicle was proceeding was seven or eight miles an hour. He heard the driver sound his horn several times after leaving Wilderspool Cro3l I no. He raw Ditchfleld standing on the roadway, and it appeared to witness as if he had hesitated when crossing the road. In his opinion, the driver did every- thing possible to avoid the accident. Williant Whitelegge, the driver, said be was going very slowly along the road, about eight or nine miles an hour. He noticed a man step off the footpath and stop in the tram lines on his (witness's) near side. Ile sounded the horn, but the man simply stood still. Wit- ness tried to get round him, when the man threw up his arms and tumbled in front of the car, which struck him on the head. Witness applied both brakes, and the car swerved with the sudden stoppage. In reply to the foremnn ot the jury, witness said it was possible thst Ditchfleld slipped when he threw up his arms.
The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," and exonerated the driver from all blame.

The Coroner expressed 'agreement with the verdict. He said he knew the difficulties with which chauffeurs had to contend, and it reflected great credit on White- legge that he held a licence which was perfectly clean.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

The funeral took place at Hill Cliffe churchyard on Wednesday afternoon, amid many expressions of deepest sympathy. The brethren of the R.A.0.8. formed a procession in regalia and walked in front of the cortege. The services in the church and at the graveside were very impressive. The deceased was borne by eight of his mother lodge brethren of the R.A.0.8., namely, Primos J. A. Woodhead, G. C. Hamblett, G. W. Taylor, H. Drummond, G. Hazlehurst. H. Ryder, and Bros. W. Tole and Z. Raynor. "Sir " James Walsh officiated as chaplain, and" Sir " Thomas Davies fulfilled the duties of marshal. Many beautiful floral tributes were received from relatives and friends, The funeral arrangements were in the hands of Mr. T. Dayies, jun., Cookhedge-lane.

div.head: JOYS OF ICE-YACHTING.
div.p: THE JOYS OF ICE-YACHTING.

Having spent a part of the winter camping in Morocco, says a writer in Country Life, we re- turned to England too early, and, seeking winter sports somewhat off the beaten track, by a lucky chance went to Sweden, where we found not only ski-running, skating, and tobogganing were to be obtained, but what will be to many the best of all, ice-yachting and skate-sailing. For excitement and exhilaration it is doubtful if there is anything to beat these sports, and for those who love pace I feel confident that there is nothing to touch them, for the speed is at the rate of the wind. The chief centre in Sweden for ice-yachting, as well as for skate-sailing, is on the large fiord called Stora Varton, just out- side Stockholm, an immense sheet of water stretching for miles, dotted with numerous birch and pine-clad islands. A more

PERFECT CRUISING - GROUND than this could, scarcely be. Usually there is ample wind to render sailing delightful, and often enough to make it of all sports the most, exciting. The Ice Yacht Club House is at Djurs- holm, on this fiord, and here lie, as a rule, some fifty boats or more, Sunday being the day for the sport. Then everywhere are sails, yachts, and skaters flying in and out of the islands. Ice- yachting, unlike boat-sailing; is quickly and readily learnt; certainly it calls for skill and muchjudgment when it comes to racing,_but with any knowledge of sailing, or even without, cruising can be cteinyed.

Bent presided, and ttere were also present :—Mrs Simpson, Miss Broadbent, Mrs. Hall, Rev. A. .M. Mitchell, Messrs. A. J. Jolley, G. Mather, W. Furness, R. Lee, W. Flanagan, M. W. Seton, J. Robinson, J. A. Hughes, F. McKinley, W. C. Brooks, A. Bottornley (clerk), W. J. Brown (master), C. E. Lowrance (super- intendent, of the Cottage Homes).
HOSPITAL AND TELEPHONE. LICCTORS ON DELAYS WHICH HAVE BEEN "NEARLY FATAL."

Drs. A. Hodgkinaon and W. Megaw drew the atten- tion of the House Committee to their report of November 28th, 1912, and the recommendations therein. They understood that those recommendations were passed by the committee and the Board. As the hospital was likely to be without a resident dcctor for some time this summer, during holidays, they again urged that telephonic communication be established with the hospital to the central, co that the enormous delay which occurred on every occasicn on which the hospital required medical assistance, or on which telephone messages reached them, might be obviated, especially at night time. Several times recently this delay had been nearly fatal to the patients concerned.
The Clerk was instructed to obtain a price for the fixing of telephonic communication between the hoipital and Dr. Hodgkinson's bouse.

Mr. MATHER corisidered that the doctors were magnifying the difficulties with regard to telephonic communication. They might draw it a little more mildly. The Guardians understood the question very well, without all those big words being put in. The minutes were approved. ASSISTANT AUDITOR'S CRITICISMS. SHARP RETORT.

The House C3mmittee considered the report made to the Local Government Board by Mr. P. T. Turner, assistant district auditor,af ter his audit of the accounts of the Workhouse, with reference to the stock of clothing and materials. They recommended that the Local Government Board be informed that the Guardians were responsible for the administration of the Workhouse and were satisfied that it was being economically conducted. When the assistant auditor had any useful suggestions to offer (the committee added) they would be pleased to receive and consider them.

The Cottage Homes Committee also considered the report as it effected their institution. The Clerk was instructed to inform the Local Government Board that, in the opinion of the Guardians, the stocks of clothing and materials at the end of the September half year, 1912, were not excessive, and that the present stocks were very low. Regarding the question of diet, the Guardians found that the following report made by

the assistant district auditor is altogether indirect : "No returns to store appear to be made by the various foster mothers who draw from stores the full scale rations for the children under their care." The foster mothers did not draw the full scale rations, and
that fact was clearly shown in the provisions 'book which was presented to the asbistant auditor at the audit.
The minutes were ftgreed to.

LIVERPOOL CATHEDRAL. ----- How the Work of Erection is Progressing. GOAL IN SIGHT.
Summer Holidays IN

The Bishop of Liverpool, presiding at a meeting of the new Cathedral Committee on Monday, said that since the scheme was launched twelve years ago half a million of money had been raised. This wonderful response has been entirely spontaneous, without pressure and entirely without recourse to unworthy means. The Lady Chapel, opened three years ago, had been described by a high authority as the most beautiful ecclesiastical building of modern times in England, and it was not too much to say that it had captured the diocese at first sight, had givin great impetus to the Cathedral movement, and in its short life had done much to unify and inspire the diocese. WARRINGTON'S SPIRITUAL CENTRE.

- Warrington and Wigan, whose affinities were,perhaps, rather with Manchester than with Liverpool, looked to it as a spiritual centre. Southport, a large proportion of whose people were interested in other dioceses, had felt its attraction. St. Helens, Widnes, Ormskirk and Earlestown were all beginning to speak of "Our Cathedral." Now they were within sight of their goal. Within four years' time the choir of the Cathedral would be opened, and the generosity of one of the most munificent of their supporters, Mr. Arthur Earle, had made it possible for the original scheme to be txtended, so that they would be able to build a tran- sept as well as a choir, and have at once a tnilding capable of holding between two and three thousand people. In addition to his former large subscriptions, Mr. Earle had offered to give £lO,OOO if £40,000 could be raised. A sum of £41,549 was needed to finish the choir and transept, and he had no doubt that sum would be forthcoming. There was still a good deal of money to be raised, the Bishop added. They ought to have a fabric fund of £40,000 in order to keep the magnificent building in thorough repair, and for a full Chapter of km Canons a very large endowment would be needed. The organ, which was being erected as a result of a handsome donation by a certain lady, would be the finest in the world.

Speaking at the close of the meeting, in reply to a vote of thanks, the Bishop mentioned that the Cathedral would be the only one in Europe built by laymen. Flom beginning to end the laymen bad taken the matter in band, and they were carrying it to a successful conclusion.

div.head: WONDERFUL WESSEX
div.p: WONDERFUL WESSEX
A splendid suggestion: Spend your Holiday in Thomas Hardy's Country.

The whole area of the Hardy country seems to breathe beauty; the three counties of Dorsetshire, Somersetshire and -Wiltshire that combine to give us "Wonderful Wessex'' are entrancingly lovely, and if the visitor be a sportsman, or if he be a devotee of any of the arts, he will find more than passing interest in this glorious Western country.

div.head: WHEN THERE WILL BE NO POOR.
div.p: WHEN THERE WILL BE NO POOR.

The 111/1,;(-Oit --S-etid--iheiir---V-va-ti every reason uhy Guardians arid Town Councils should be linked together in friendly work. However, under the operations of the Insurance 'Act, Si bich covered everyone until the age of seventy, when the old age pension was received, he was afraid there would very soon he no poor for the Guardians to operate upon. (Laughter.) That was doubtless one reason why, in their admirable new buildings, they were doing all they could to preserve the lives of the people under their care, for fear they should never get any more. (Laughter.) Retorting to the manifold duties of a Mayor, his Worship attributed ignorance on the point to the fact that successive occupants of the chair, instead of exposing their grievances, found themselves too busy to alltoe to them, and when they had retired they were plunged into obscurity and people did not care about listening to them. (Laughter.) He did not know any clays of man who had to pei form more important duties with- out previous special education, than he who undertook the position of Meyer. On that ground it would be a very good thing if the deputy-mayor, instead of being a former occupant of the Mayoralty, were selected from the general body of the Council,with a vi)w this ulti- mate election to the office of Mayor. He would then be able to gain some education as to the duties.
WARRING lON COMPARED WI ill OTHER I\iUNICIPALITIES.

_ Comparing Warrington with other municipalities which he had visited, his Worship said there were very few Council Chambers which were as large, in ratio to the number of mem- bers, es the Warrirgten Council Chamber, although that was a small one. In other towns little or no provision was ma-le for the general public to attend the meetings. lie had also ascertained that Town Council meetings in other Lancashire boroughs, as a rule, occupied a very shert space of time. 1113 friends of the Press would no doubt like to live there. (Laughter.) In some places, the meetings were regarded as exceptionally long if they lasted an hour. It might be said that they in Warrington took to,r much time over their rueetinga, but, after all, it was a good quality that they did not deal with their work in a, slipshod manner, and if there were sometimes critical and actimonious speeches, they gave credit to those who made them for desiring only the -public good. (Hear, heir.) It looked as if the members of the Council took an interest in their work and had the well- being of their constituents at hlart, when they t )ok so much trouble wider' Ili .y might easily avoid if they followed the practcei in vogue in other places. There wereconAucled his Worshi:-Atnany worse Councils than the Warrington Town Council.

div.head: HOW _THE RATES ARE INCREASED,
div.p: HOW _THE RATES ARE INCREASED,

Alderman Slat ETnu-nwr, who also responded, claimed that the Town Council had not increased the actual normal rates of the borough during the last thirty 3 ears, although they hal made improvements at a rapid rate. lhe 0 uncil a ere not to blame for the advancing expenditure, as much of it was due to the erection of new schools, the cost of education and the widening of old streets. The money had not been wasted although there was a variety of opinion on the questien of education. There was a strong impression among the public that we were not on the right path in the Hucation of the children,but that too many duties which might be left to the parents wore being undertaken by the authorities. Children of sixteen nowadays thought they knew a great deal more than their parents and consequently were impudent towards them. That was not the way in which the rising generation should be brought up. Alderman Smethurst concluded by referring to the great work in the fight against con- sumption, which it was hoped to do at the Sankey Sanatorium, and said the Corporation were willing to do their utmost to work in harmony with the Board of Guardians in efforts of that kind. (Applause.) lie believed it was thirty-two years since the Corporation I first began to concern itself about the widening of W.r- rington Bridge—(laughter)--but they were now within measurable distance of the completion of the new bridge—in fact when the engineer toll him the probable date, he replied, "If you finish it in that time I will buy you a new hat." (Laughter.) Mr. J. BACKHOUSE proposed "The Building Com- mittee," and Mr. G. MATHER responded. Ile described the Warrington Workhouse as one of the most up-to- date institutions of its kind in Great, Britain.

Mr. W. FURNESS proposed "Our Visitors." Alderman JOHN EVANS, in responding, said the way in which the inmates of the Workhouse were attended to was a credit to the Board. As a ratepayer, he did not regret one penny of his instalment of the cost of the improvements. (Applause.)

div.head: WARRINGTON AND THE MERSEY.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND THE MERSEY.

Councillor BIRTLKS also responded, and said he was astonished at the alterations which had taken place at the institution of recent years. They chplored the fact that,people should have to enter the Workhouse, but the Guirdians did their best to make the lives of these unfortunate classes—some of whom were there through no fault of their own —as comfortable and happy as possible. Alluding to municipal ear tirs, the speaker said there never was a time iu the history of Warrington when the work which confronted the Corporation was so great as to-day. (Hear, hear.) He regretted that the to:vn had not yet taken full advantage of its natural asset—the river Mersey—but he hoped the Corporation would move in that matter before long. Such a development, taken in conjunction with the projected extension of the borough boundaries, would result in the revival of ship-building, and the setting up of more great industries within our midst. (Applause.) Mr. Plume C. GARNgrr proposed "The architects
LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR WIDNES. SPEECH BY MR. J. B. MARTIN DALE.

Mr. J. B. Martindale, the prospactive Liberal candi- date for the Widnes Division, addressed a very large open-air meeting at Widnes on Saturday night. His main theme was the Insurance Act Amendment LW, which, he said, fully covered the main objections to the Act, and it remained to be seen whet the attitude of the critics would be. Mr. Martindale afterwards answered a large number of qty..stions dealing with various phases of the Act. Mira Andersen (a graduate of Liverpool University) a,,ked the speaker a series of questions as to his views on the suffrage question. His reply was an unqualified approval of the principal of votes for women, and he assured his questioner that when hi 3 election address was published that would be seen plainly. Ile had always deprecated the tactics of the militants, because hi) believed that they had been puttirg back the cause. Ile had always been in favour of the principle, because ha believed it was based on common justice. Answering a question as to low wages, Mr. Martin- dale said that if returned to Parli imebt be would support the principle of a minimum wage, and if his pity (Id not bring in a Minimum Wage Bill, he him- self would do so. At the close of the n-Teting thee cheers for Mr. Martineale were given spontanee nsly.
RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB. IMPROVED FINANCIAL POSITION.
The annual general nveting of the Runcorn Football Club, Limited, vtas held in Orcenway-road Schools on Nlonday, N. J. Littler, preeiding over a fair attendance of members.

The Chairman said the club had gone through a very trying year. Naturally, those shareholders who did not receive a dividend wore disappointed, but there was a feeling of satisfaction among them when they became acquainted with the club's financial position. The shares were not taken up with the zral that the security warranted, and consequently a heavier interest fell upon those who had taken up the sharer. It was a new venture. Ile was sorry to see there was a loss on the schoolboy c)mpetitions, but be hoped the directors would not be discouraged, and whin the time came they would entertain tie question of twining the competitions again. The loss of £9O wh;ch the club had sustained in the 191142 season bad been reduced by £IO, which was tie profit on the past season's working. Tie report was adopted. A resolution, proposed by Mr. J. Littlar, and seconded by Mr. J. Shaw, was carried unanimously empower- ing the directors to borrow £3OO to complete the new ground.

div.head: Opening ofi New Dining-Hall, Kitchen and Bakery.
div.p: Opening ofi New Dining-Hall, Kitchen and Bakery.
MAYOR'S COUNCIL COMPARISONS.

The completion of an extensive scheme of structural improvements at the Warrington Workhouse wa celebrated on Monday, when the new dining-halls kitchen and bakery were formally opened by the Chairman of the Board of Guardians (Mr. Edward L. Beta). The inmates have enjoyed the comfort of the enlarged and up-to-date dining accommodation since Chtistmas, but the opening ceremony was deferred until the whole of the alterations, which include the erection of a ferro-concrete water tower, had been carried out. Lofty and well-lighted, the new dining hall is in every way adapted for its purpose, and the transformation, as compared with the old conditions, is iudeed striking. The kitchen is fitted with the l-itest typo of pans and steamers, while the bakehouse has patent draw- plate ovens and electtic dough-mixeis. no water tower has a capacity of 18,000 gallons, and it will provide a high pressure supply for use in the laundries and tramp wards, as well as to cone with any outbreak of fire that might arise. The entire scheme has cost close upon £5,000. Messrs. W. and A. Ashton, Bridge Felt, have erected the buildings to the designs of Messrs. William and Segar Owen, Cairo-street.

There was a large attendance of Guardians, ex-members of the Boatd, representatives ( f the Corpotation and other well-known townspeiple at the opening ceremony. When the company had assembled in the dining-hall, the Rev. W. Bracecacap (chaplain) offered prayer..

PRESENTATION OF GOLD KEY. Mr. SEGAR OWEN, en behalf of the architects presented Mr. Bent with a beautiful gold commemora- tion key. Mr. G. MATEIER, chairman of the Building mittee, then invited Mr. Bent, as representing the Board and the ratepayers to take over the custody of the new buildings, which, he said, would supply a bug-felt want. The scheme had given rise to much thought and anxiety but, with the help of their architects, they had brought it to a very successful conclusion. (Applause.) Mr. BENT, in declaring the buildings open, said that for some considerable time the dining-room, kitchen and baking accommodation had been most inadequate, and most of the cooking apparatus was beyond repair. Alterations had repeatedly been made to cope with the difficulty, but it was found that, in order to meet present needs, larger premises were required, and the present scheme was embarked upon. The dining- ball was not large enough to accommodate all the inmates, and ether places had to be used as dining rooms. The new scheme would obviate that incon- venience. The cooking apparatus and baking ovens were of the very latest designs, and be was satisfied that the money had been wisely spent. (Hear, hear.) TLe work of the architects and o ntractors had given every satisfaction to the Board._ ( pplause.)
IIIE MAYOR'S CONGRATULATIONS,
The MAYOR (Councillor 11-.. Joseph) congratulated

the Board on the success which Gad crow7ned their efforts, and exprcssed himself astounded at the trans- formation elli!ch had been effected in the buildings. lie hoped the alterations would concime to the comfort and happiness of the inmates of the institution.

(Applause.) Mr. A. J. JoLLEY (deputv-chbirman of tha Board) said that all who had been concerned in the improve- ments had given of their best, aid the results must afford them groat gratification. No one had taken a keener personal interest, or had more highly appre- ciated the good work done than the Chairman of the Board. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Jolley concluded by pro- posing a vote of thinks to the arelitects and contrac- tors for the excellent way in which they had carried out th 3 scheme. -
Mr. MATHER seconded, and the vote was heartily accorded. - -

_ The company then took the opportunity of inspect- ing the new buildings, which were generally admired The visitors were also conducted through the hospital, and were very favourably impressed with the provision made for the comfort of the sick poor.

div.head: DINNER AT THE LION HOTEL.
div.p: DINNER AT THE LION HOTEL.

Later there was a highly successful gathering at the Lion Hotel,when Mr. Bent entertained a large assembly at dinner. The catering of Mr. John Lee gave every satisfaction. "SUCCE3S TO THE NEW BUILDING."

Mr. BENT, who presided, proposed" Success to the new building." He pointed out that the dining-hall, kitchen, and bakery had been built in close touch on the same floor, and that would be a great corenience to the staff who had to wait upon the inmates. The Guardians were almost afraid to tamper with the old buildings, lest they might collapsp, but all difficulties had been overcome, and now they had a set of buildings which was second to none in Lancalhire. (Applause.) RATES NOT RAISED FOR MANY YEARS.

Mr. G. MATHER. responded. He regarded the scheme as one of the greatest 8110025908 which the WarringVn Board of Guardians had achieved for many years. Ile believed those who had inspected the buildings would agree that the Board was cne of the most progressive in this part of the country. (Applause.) They had carried out the improvement without touching the ratepayers' pockets. During the many years he had been a Guardian, they had not raised the rates one penny, thanks to some of the officials and the way in which they had manipulated the loans at low interest. 'rho health of the inmates of the Workh9u3e was at present " A 1." They were always ready for their food, because it was well cooked, appetising and well served. (Applause.)

div.head: AN ECONOMICAL SCHEME.
div.p: AN ECONOMICAL SCHEME.

Mr. W. FURNICSS also responded. No doubt the rate- payers would have considered it a greater success if the new buildings had not been required at all. Under the circumstances, however, the best they could do was to provide premises which would be equal to the stress which times of poverty and hardship might produc The new buildings, had been oonstruct2d on the most economical lines. Under the old conditions the ovens cost 303. a week to work, but in the new kitchcn the experse would be only 10E. a week. There would thus be a saving of something like £.50 a year—almost sufficient to provide interest and sinking fund for the improvement. It was anticipated that a further saving would be effected by the use of the new water tower. The Guardilns claimed that they were doing all theycould to lengthen the lives of the people committed to their care. It -might be more expen.,,ive to the ratepayers, but it was part of the Board's policy. If parental duties were better realised in some quarters, there would be far less expenditure on the Poor Law. (Hear, hear.)
" TUE MAYOR AND CORPORATION."
MR. JOLLEY'S HUMOROUS COMMENTS ON ROYAL VISIT PREPARATIONS.

Mr. A. J, JOLLEY proposed "The Mayor and Corpora- tion of Warrington." Ile said he understood that the difficulties with which the Mayor had had to contend in connection with the arrangements for the Royal visit were such as to try the patience of a professional archangel, let alone of an ordinary Mayor. (Laughter.) tie was also told that those who had the good fortune or otherwise to he in front of the Town Hall on Monday would see some marvellous creations of sartorial art decorating the persons of some of the more eminent members of their beloved Corporation. (Laughter.) He believed many tailors and tailoresses were seriously exercised by the difficult feats which were required of them to meet the demands, of the occasion. (Lsughter.) However highly they might esteem and love the members of the Corporation an impartial observer could not justly claim that they were all designed, anatomically and physically, in accordance with the rules of classic Greek art. (Laughter.) The surmounting of the difficulties pre- sented to the ordinary tailor and tailoress in success- fully clothing the physical features of some of our public representitives, might be justly regarded as a triumph of art. (Laughter.) He understood that some of the creations could not be entrusted to local pro- fessionials, but that even Paris bad been called into requisition. (Laughter.)

div.head: "WISE AND OTHERWISE."
div.p: "WISE AND OTHERWISE."

It must be admitted that all the members of the Corporation were wise. (Laughter.) Of course, they were wise with a difference. Some of them were wise and some were otler-wise. (Laughter.) Guardians, as members of a public authority knowing that the usual reward of disinterested service to the public consisted in receiving more kicks than halfpence, must have some sympathy for the Town Councillors who bad to undergo the same process. He was afraid that, however desir- able it might be that it should he otherwise, they had not all got the fear of God in their hearts, but most members of public authorities had the fear of the rate- payers when election time came—(laughter)—and were occasionally tempted to play to the gallery, and even to sacrifice those higher interests which in their better moments, they all had at heart. THE SENSE OF SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY.

_ During the last twenty-five years a very great change had come over the spirit of public life in this country. There bad been an expanding conception of social responsibility, which, on the whole, was a very good thing fur the community. Doctrines which thirty-five years ago were regarded as absolutely sacrosanct were now brushed aside—and ci isely so. The old doctrines of extreme individualism, the doctrines proclaimed by Cobden and Bright fifty years ago, and which, when he was a boy, were regard( d as rather superior to the canonical gospels—(laughter)— had been swept aside. We now went in for Factory Acts, legislation with regard to education, and in many other directions for the improvements of social con- .

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday, Mr. C. E. Linaker presiding.
INSPECTION OF HOUSES.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board stating that the Board had observed the action taken in regard to the inspection of houses under the Housing and Town Planning Act, as mentioned in the Medical Officer's annual report, and asking whether it was not possible to expedite the inspection. The matter was referred to the Housing and Town Planning Committee, the Clerk observing that the work of their committee would compare tavourably with that of any other District Council in the country.

div.head: "A NEAR THING."
div.p: "A NEAR THING."

The Clerk read the result of tbe by-election in Clifton. The result was :—Joseph Stokes, 20 votes; John Henry Davies, six votes. Mr. Mclntyre: A very near go. (Laughter.) he Chairman : We shall all be pleased to see the son of one of our oldest members with U 3. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: TOWN PLANNING.
div.p: TOWN PLANNING.

The Clerk and Mr. Woodward, the delegates from the Council, read reports of the Housing and Town Planning Conference, which they hid attended. Mr. Woodward instanced the rapid strides which Liverpool had made in this direction.
It was decidel that the Clerk endeavour to procure copies of the papers read at the Conference.
TIIE Sr. HELENS MURDER INQUEST.

On Monthy, at St. Helens, a coroner's jury returned a verdict of wilful murder against James Kerrigan, who out the throats of his wife Susan, aged 45, and his son Harry, aged five, as they lay in led asleep on Thursday morning last. In the case of Kerrigan himself, who died after cutting his own threat, a verdict of suicide was returned. The jury added that there was no evidence to show the state of the man's mind. Kerrigan had complained of his wife's drunken habits and her neglect of the boy.

Some Startling Announcements that
Must be Read with Care.
WONDERS OF INGENIOSITY.

How endurable is the good feeling that now exists between the French people and the English people is attested by the fact that our friendship has survivea the way in which we have persistently murdered each other 's language for ages. Mr. H. M. Ashton sends us the following, which throws into high relief the cordial welcome we have just given to the President of the nation that claims the author for a citizen : • We have recently come across an interesting booklet entitled "Practical guide of the Exhibition, Paris, 1880," writtn by a Frenchman for the guidance of English visitors to the Exhibition, which contains some very choice examples of literal translation from the French.

The preface opens thus : "The Universal Exhibition, for whom who comes there for the first time, is a true chaos in which it is impossible to direct and recognise one's self without a guide. To reach this aim we have divided our itineraries or excursion at the Exhibition, in days, of which each one is farming a chapter. May the visitor follow us with confidence and he will not have any reason to regret it." This is a good s-art, and now we proceed to the idea of the Exhibition. "It was in the air several years, when divers newsplpera, in 1883, bethought them to consecrate several articles to it and so it became a serious matter. _
The period of incubation (brooding) lasted siuce 183 S. till the month of Itiarch,lBB4."And now for the entrance.

'Constables are afte:ted in a permanent manner at the service of every wicket. The chief controller has t 3 concert bum with the Polies chief dt the Exhibition to assure the reaular execution of the Entrance." What of the Tower Eiffel?

An engineer presented him. Mr. Eiffel already known by his considerable and keen works. He proposed to M. Lecroy to erect a tower in iron, which reaching the height of 300 metres, would rep -scent, at the industrial sight, the resultant of the m)dern
progresses:' Here is a charming bird's eye view fr)ni the sumadt:-- _

_ "At the right Montmartre which seems a vessel entering in the aide of a pariscian galere. At yo tr feet the houses are very plainly, because you see th four sides which are holed by the windows, symetric like points of dice, so well that Paris has all appearauce of a vast party of biribe played by a giant on a green carpet, seventeen hundred eighty twelve steps bring you to the top ! " Proceeding onwards we come to the fountain under tie tower and find this pithy description of the figures:— "Europe, under the lines of a woman, leane t upon a printing press to print and a book, seems deeped in profound reflections." " as.merica is a young woman, enelgetic and virginal however, characterising the youth and the atielacies of the American people."

But Asia, lie! fie ! - "Asia, the craddle of the human kind, represents the volupty and the sensualisan. Her posture, the pi.Lsion ut her figw o tenuer well the ..nandunineut of t'..o passion with the oriental people." Having g,-,ized with admiration on the wonderful works of art, we are directed to take our first walk round the exhibition : "Thus we begin, at present as we have let him see thesa 2 wonderworks which fly at the eyes, the Tower and the fountain, to return on his steps to retake with order this walk of recogniti.m which will permit him, thanks to our watchfulness to see all in a short time." We must see this, certainly : One of the most smart attractions of the exhibition, which is one of the most remarkable, is the musical indian c'iorus of the bishoprick of Para, composed of a 150 executors, native women of Amazure." _ _

Here is a case of revoking, evidently : We have remoted us. Let us come back to the right and in front and higher up the French Eating- house, we shall see placed across, the monumental pavilion of Venezuela, at the white turrets and at the picturesque decorations." The remarks about the palace of the children pique our curiosity : " It is M. Emile Ullmann, great price of Rome in

_ IS7I who has created this splendid palace, and he has certainly succeeded in making of it a wonder of elegancy and ingeniosity. When they had built there a theatre destined to amuse our little minions, M. Alphs,nd comes to say, we have not a serious theatre at the Exhibition. Give us your scene. In such way that this palace is also called Great Theatre of the Exhibition. Enter there with your little family and you will certainly not annoy you, your babies will 'find there a kermess with a shooting for macaronis, turnpikes divers games, wafles and milk." Now Mr. Eiffel comes in for a little criticism : "Pavilion Eiffel, at the left and forward at the first

left foot of the tower a small pavilion surmounted with cupolas which give to it an aspect half oriental, half quite what you like." This last phrase is rich, isn't it? We must see the Pavilion of Monaco, however : " When vou will be on the flight of steps before the entrance of the Fine Arts, which is ill front of the Seine, you will have on your right the Pavilion of Monaco, pretty construction which expresses well the character of this principality of green carpet." Don't let us miss the chemistry section :

"In going out from the domain of the hongrery and tannery we penetrate in that of the chemistry and apothicarery as it is raid in jesting the art to drug the people." "Then come the spungeA, corals, until coales representing the products of fishing."

Note this : "To be temarked an enorm trunk of mahogany high almost 5 metres." Surely we ought to skip this "Finally merceries, morning gowns which would give an envy never to see the ladies but undressed, and petticoats which are true meals, stays, braces and garters, worthy of a young bride." Our guide *axes sarcastic, as thus "Finally the shoes for both sexes in which one remarks shoes, which without doubt, have been placed there by forgetfulness, for they would have been better at their place in the pavilion of the navigation in the part reserved to the small boats ! " To understand this description of the Pavilion of retrospective History of Work and Sciences is harder than evolving "Bounties" : " All the cJnstruction is in 1100 l of fir trees- Its

decoration is of simple style and absolutely original. On a green bottom whose tonality is harmonious by black and white rebauts, bronze and gold, detach, them of the decorative massives of a. delicate drawing borrowed from the ornamental flare." We give it up! and proceed to the hall for the exhibition of musical instruments. Our guide has evidently been upset by this exhibit, for he says: " Unfortunately all this harmony is lost in the enormous noise produced by so many melodious machines or not. The bass instruments burst, the organs roar the pianos mourn, and the violins mew, without counting the orchestrions which commence to acclimate them in France, which is not a recommen- dation and of which some ones are monuments." Referring to an exhibition of furniture by a well- known house, we get this gem : Is it necessary to say that this incomparable house defies any other by the modieity of its prices ? Truly, all these things are at the reach of the leas profligate parses ! We must linger awhile at the perfumery depart- ment, for " The perfumery is dependent and is announced by delicious efiluvias. There is on show all known and unknown cosmetics, violet and all the perfumes at fashion have there their exhibitions which charm the eyes in balming you the smell." Let us have a look at Japan : " We arrive at Japan. Our walk will redouble of interest, the exottsot of this singular country being well made to astonish the friends of wonders. The Japanese section is very vast. What to say of it ? What to cite? All is unheard there, huperb, unlikely. Yid° has sent vases whi2ll are true jewels, glasses, furnitures, in lakes, in bronze, screams originally painted. Kioto exhibits tea caddies in silver, recovered, enamelled without equals." A view of the street of Csito is evidently better than a sedlitz powder : " It was famous in Paris much before the opening of the Exhibition, this picturesque street. When one. comes out of the palace of the divers industries, a little giddy pate and aching of a blustering decoration, the eyes rest them there instantly." We must be very careful when we come to the "Yard of the motor's force" : " Before to cross this dedale of machines which

whistle, spit the vapour, burn and roar in unison, you wish without doubt to know which force makes more these thousands of connecting rods and excentriques. It is there behind the palace, what they call the yard of motor's force."

The English machinery is damned with faint praise : " The English machine have a pretty large reputa- tion and certainly there are among those exhibited here which deserve the attention, but not any is 'prominent nor fix the curiosity." In the lighting department we are told that— " Tne gaso-multiplex is the smallest economical burner which one knows. Its construction is of a simplicity such as it dispenses of all care. The gas being no more warm and arriving from up and down, not any deposit, nor any obstruction could be pro- duced. Moderate price of the apparatus. Economy of gas 100 c." From a great way off we must view the pavilioa of forests and rivers, for we are told : "From far, the columns, with their coverings formed by oaks, beeches, whole maples, not the bark peeled off, resemble to the marble, at certain places, for better to ressort the differences, they placed pannels the one near the other, of sound wood and others attacked by parasit insects. Impossible to push farther on the passion of the natural. " The aquarium is a great attraction: These troughs of the capacity of 25 metres each are disposed on concentrie ranks of underground galleries, presenting to the visitor mirrors through which he can see the fishes take their gambols. Each is surmounted by an etiket which bears the name of its inhabitants."

Faith in the Havannah cigar shattered. Referring to the exhibition of tobac:ms and cigars we read this : "However, it wants much that all the cigars manu- factured at Havanah are good. All the conaissors are at the contrary, in one accord concerning the decay the more to more accentuaced of the tobaces of Havanah, and declare that the true puvo which has its excellent aroma, curites an agreeable taste and a regular com- bustion, becomes the more to more rare and dearer."

The Javanese get it straight from the shoulder : " The Javanese are short, have the legs arched and frail. They have a lazzy and iudolent nature easy to be led. Very jealous they serve them of the least pretext of their dreadful Khrist kind of dagger which they bear habitually at the girdle." Neither are the Tonkins complimented : . _ _

"The Tonkinis have likewise a-flat figure, are flat nosed, squat at the begining, the eyebrows badly shaped and little thick. They smoke much, chew some betel, nourish them with rice, with rotted fish, with dogs, brooden eggs or likewise rotted. Their religion is tne boudhism, a little changed. " The Tahitian village has many charms :-- " The ial tr.d of Tahiti which enjoys of an almost eternal spring, is so picturesque, so poetic that its charms are found in its inhabitants. The Tahitians are distingtuished by a beauty of the shapes, by a stature above the middle one and an expression of the figure very meek. The men are girdling their flanks and legs with a cotton piece called paren and hear on their torso an European shirt whose sides are floating in the air."—There's a picture for you ! For a cheap meal we must go toi the palace of the social economy : "At the left of the principal palace and hard by is a building in planks where the philantropical society has installed s model economical store. Therein is a room of coszsornitiations whose prices very much reduded are sticked at the door. It is coquettish and quiet and one would like to inhabit there ! " Gabon, a French colony on the coast of Guinea, is represented by a village, and seems to possess some fairly large insects:— " The collection of insects of Gab•n is one of the most instructive.To cite the dreadful red ant and which replaces there the erring dogs of Constantinople, charged to clean the streets of all uncleanness. When these little beasts attack a small village, in a few days it has disappeared." Now for the peroration : " There is finished our common walk, and in a happy way, after six days which, we dare believe it, did not seem to you long and tiresome, your cariosity finding a constant aliment at every step which we made you do, in this exhibition without rivalry. Where the beauties succeeded to the beauties where one leaves not one pleasure but for a new one. As for us our task of cicerone is agreeable to us, that we shall do our best to retain you still near us in efforc- ing us to discover still other spectacles and, to present you them after all those you know already. H. AI. ASHTON.

div.head: MODERN PILGRIMAGE.
div.p: THE MODERN PILGRIMAGE.
Constitutional, Anti-Militant Suffragists Who Are Heading for London. PEACEABLE, BUT ATTRACTIVE.
[BY A LIDY CORRESPONDTiNT.]

The Woman Suffrage pilgrimage to London is the biggest thing in demonstrations ever attempted by a Suffrage Society. Only the National Union with its 44,000 members and 400 branches would dream of such an enterprise, and its successful organisation is another instance of women's capabilities as stage and business managers. Already women from the North and West have begun the march, which will end in Hyde Park on July 20, and already some 40 or 50 meetings have been held in the towns through which the pilgrims have passed. Young and old, rich and ppor, will, during the next few weeks, walk side by side to demonstrate the strength and determination of Suffragists, and those who cannot march the whole way are giving up a week, a day or even a few hours in order that they may take some part in this wonderful demonstration. • There are three main objects in this pilgrimage. First, the advertising of non-militant Suffragism ; second, the carrying of the Suffrage arguments through- out the length and breadth of England ; third, the raising of a large sum of money, in order to make it quite clear that this is a demonstration by anti- militants every pilgrim is required to wear a red, white and green badge in her bat as a symbol that she belongs to, or is in sympathy with, the National Unoiu, the great constitutional body of Suffragists.

div.head: LADY MAYOR AND CARAVAN PARTY.
div.p: LADY MAYOR AND CARAVAN PARTY.

The special offering in connection with the pilgrim- age has already amounted to £2,000, nearly all of which has been given in comparatively small sums. The only big donation conies from Miss Lees,daughter of Oldham's Lady Mayor (who, by the way, is doing the pilgrimage with eleven other ladies in caravans ! ). Only two conditions are laid on pilgrims. The first is the undertaking to wear the non-militant badge; and the second, that they must proceed by road, not rail. It is not intended, however, that those taking part should be obliged to walk and walk only. Bicycles and motor cars are permitted, and one or more of the latter will accompany most sections and act as baggage waggons and occasionally as transports. Tne Watling-street route, which will be adopted by Lancashire and Cheshire pilgrims, lies through Chester, Nantwich, Stafford, Birmingham, and Oxford, at all of which points other bands of pilgrims will join in and swell the numbers. On July sth there will be a grand send-off from Liverpool, at which a good many War- rington Suffragists are expected to be present. The send-off will take the form of a procession from the Suffrage office to the Exchange Flags, where a short meeting will be held, after which the pilgrims, accom- panied by sympathisers, will march to the landing stage, and there take the boat to Birkenhead and thence the road to Chester. A VAST UNDERTAKING. •

It is impossible to calculate the effect this vast undertaking will have on the country at large, but it is safe to assume that for once the law-abiding Suffragists will attract as much attention as the militants, and the sight of so many women sacrificing their money and personal comfort in order to further the Suffrage movement is, of itself, likely to make people consider the question seriously. The dernonstratioo, which will take place in Hyde Park on July 20th at the end of the pilgrimage, will be on an enormous scale. Eighteen platforms are already arranged for, and the assembled crowds are likely to assume huge proportions. The next day, Sunday, the majority of the pilgrims will attend the afternoon service at St. Paul's, there, as Mrs. Fawcett has put it, " to renew our purpose of self-dedication, aud to learn from the mighty dead around us, what long enduring hearts can do."

div.head: PROMISED EDUCATION BILL.
div.p: THE PROMISED EDUCATION BILL.
In the House of Commons on Wednesday, Sir P. Magnus asked when the Education Bill would be introduced. _ _ _

Mr. Asquith replied that he could not say more at present than that at an early date the President of the Board of Education would make a full statement of the intentions and policy of the Goveinmmt in regard to education.

div.head: JUSTICE, NOT CHARITY,
div.p: JUSTICE, NOT CHARITY,
How The Liberal Government is Helping to Raise The Masses.

TORIES' SLANDEROUS CAMPAIGN. There was an exceedingly large assembly at the weekly mesting of the Progressive Labour League at Bridge Foot on Monday. Mr. W. H. Sherburn presided. and the principal speaker was Mr. T. H. Garside, of Manchester, who is very popular with Warrington audiences. He speaks forcefully, and brightens his addresses with a wealth of humour. He devoted him- self to exposing the inaccurate propaecies of the Tory party in regard to the various Acts which the Liberal Government had passed. His concluding item was one of ridicule for the Tory Land campaign, which, he said, did not tend to relieve the people one iota. BRIDGES THE GOVERNMENT ARE BUILDING. ('he CITAIRMAN drew isr analogy between the new bridge and the work of I e Liberal party. He said the Government had doue t good bit of road-making and bridge-building. (Hear, hear.) But there were still many more roads to widen and bridges to make before the people received what they wanted and what they ought to have. Until all the roads had been made, the present Government ought to receive the whole- hearted support of the people of England. Justice was required for Wales, and they wou:d get it. It was also requiced for Ireland. and, in spite of all the opposition that was on loot, the Liberal party would give to Ireland that which she SD much- desired. (Applause.) Ideas only just in the initial stages would be materialised before the Govern- ment concluded their term of office, and one was the abolition of plural voting. (Applause.) He did not need to tell them much about that, as they knew the unfairness of one man having more than one vote. Then there was the good wide road to make in regard to the land monopoly, which had been long overdue. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion, he would say that the day was far past when they could ask woman to assist them in electoral matters and say she was not fit to have a vote. That was another of the roads which would have to be evidennd, and the Liberal party were the people to do all they could in, the interests of the masses of the country. (Applause.) TORY PARTY'S CAMPAIGN OF VITUPERATION.

Mr. GARSIDE said that Lord Rosebery bad said that. Old Age Pensions were the beginning of the end. That went by, and then the Tories said the Insurance Act. was the beginning of the end. "We have," joculously commented Mr. Garside, " been going headlong to ruin ever since 1906, and we were told a fortnight ago that we need no longer fear, as the Conservative party was coming back into power, that they would undo all we had done ; restore the equilibrium of the universe, and set men on their feet once more." In regard to the Tory party's attitude when the Marcaui Committee was sitting, he would have liked to put one question, and that was: " Will any of you gentlemen who are :30 anxious to see Mr. Lloyd George's bank book pro- duce your own? Where do you deal and what shares do you bold ? " The Tories had been indulging in a game of inuendo, slander, malice and vituperation. That, however, was all they could expect from the gentlemanly party._ (Laughter.)_______

_ *REDUCING, PAUPERISM. Illustrating the good work dune by the Liberal party, he said that during the last seven years they had reduced the number of recipients of pauper relief by 9G per cant. The Liberal party said that no matter how poor, ignorant, or of what birth they were, the na-m and women of the country had a right to the highest joy of life that God could provide. (Hear, h,ar.)They had been told that the Insurance Act was going to be a gigantic failure, and if it were not so tragic, that would be the funniest thing of all. The medical men had conspired, planned, dodged, squirmed and wriggled in order that the Act would not work. They now s dci that the women were malingering, but there was nat the slightest truth in the statement. Before the Insurance Act came into operation, women worked at the looms and in the cardroom up to within three days of their children being born, but there was no longer any necessity for them to do so, and consequently they were charged with malingering. £7,000 per week was being distributed in maternity benefits alone. (Applause.) Of curse, the Act was a gigantic fraud. (Laughter.) They had paid £200,000 in sick benefits and who was getting that money ?—the so-called great unwashed moo. To-day,they had 7,000 men and women in sanatoria throughout the country. (Applause.) Oh !" added Mr. Garside, "but that is not the extent of our wrongdoing. (Laughter.) We give the wives 10s. per week whilst the hushaad is in the sanatoria."

WIPING OUT THE WORD "CHARITY." The Liberal party were wiping the word " county " from the dictionary, and, in the place of it, they were putting " God-given justice. "After all the good the Liberal party had done, tbe Opposition as much as said that they could be written down as hopelessly ruined ; that soon the German flag would be floating over the Town Hill ; that we snould all be subjects of the German Empire ; and that England was going to the devil. (Laughter.) Lord Lansdowne said the only thing that could save the country was a Conservative Government. (Laughter.) Speakiug on the question of land taxation, Mr. Garside said Lord Lansdowne had said that there were 3.000,000 fewer acres under cultivation than there were 25 years ago. Where had the land gone to? Had France stolen it? He really believed those abominable Irish had dug it up and taken it home. (Laughter.) He could assure them that the greatest burden a manufac- turer bad in his business was not wages, rates, railway charges, or the cost of light, but it was the cost of land. (Hear, hear.) A twopenny tax on the value of land would bring in £71,000,C00, and they only required £35,000,000 to abolish all the taxes on the breakfast table. After further expounding the land taxation pro- posals, Mr. Garside said Lord Lansdowne spoke of his party's "reasonable and feasinle" plan for solution of the land problem. His scheme was that "B" (toe land- owner) had the land and the money ; "A " (the working classes) wanted the land and had not gut the money. The Government, a collection of all the "A's," not having the money, borrowed the money from " B " in order to buy " B's " land with " B's " money for A." (Laughter.) He (the speaker) believed Lord Lansdowne was in earnest, but he must remember that the people in the country were not fools. The Liberal party's scheme was a far better one, and was worthy of the honest and whole-hearted support of all the members of the com- munity. (Applause.) On the proposition of Mr. JOSEPH ELWELL, seconded by Mr. J. COT TERILL, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded the speaker and chairman.

div.head: F. HALLETT,
div.p: F. HALLETT,
The Jeweller & Silversmith,
10, BRIDGE ST. WARRINGTON.
MR. HAROLD SMITH, M.P., AT CORNHILL.

After a strangely protracted and unex- plained silence, Mr. HAROLD SMITH visited Warrington last week-end, and Saturday night saw him competing for a hearing ith what he called "a gentleman selling medicine," at Cornhill. The " opposition show" was quickly talked down, however, and the way cleared for the occupants of the Conservative van. Mr. SMITH spoke about himself first and last, and sandwiched in some belated remarks regarding the Insur- ance Act. the Marconi squabble and, prin- cipally, the Housing Bill produced by the Committee of which he is a distinguished member. As will be seen, it was a particu- larly lean kind of deliverance, but Mr. SMITH may generally be trusted to make up for the paucity of his subjects by the manner in which he deals with them. It was indeed a remarkably ill-natured speech, but perhaps the time and place had as much as anything to do with that. Saturday night, in Cornhill, it has to be con fessed, is not inspiring, especially when a medical gentleman, who already has possession of the pitch, has to be dis- possessed. Of course, the " shameful " conduct of the Government in refusing to allow the Opposition to ruin the chances of the passing of the principal measures of this Parliament was exposed for the edification of the Corn- hill audience. Mr. SMITH appeared to claim the right to discuss, in the House, the Insur- ance Bill for twelve months and to suggest that it did not receive that careful and pro- tracted attention because Mr. REDMOND wanted Insurance out of the way to make room for the Home Rule Bill. That is only stating the truth the wrong way about. Mr, SMITH and his friends wished the discussion to go on—apparently for twelve months —and the Home Rule Bill, after these long years of waiting, would have been effectually scotched. That the Government saw through the ruse and prevented its success is no doubt " shameful " in the eyes of Mr. SMITH; but other people other adjec- tives. The Insurance Act is still troubling Mr. SMITH on the " mandate " side of the question. National Insurance was by no means a new question and it was understood that the earlier Liberal Budgets, which so

upset the mental equilibrium of the privileged, were designed to provide the wherewithal to carry through a series of overdue social reforms. But assuming that Insurance was not foreshadowed in the Liberal programmes, do Governments always wait for mandates in the narrow sense that Mr. SMITH uses the word? Did the Conservatives have a mandate to place the elementary education of the country in the hands of the Church of England in 1902? Or, to come to the doings of this "shameful" Government, had they definite instructions to give Mr. SMITH a salary of £4OO a year? At the close, Mr. SMITH was asked whether he 'is,‘ -ould help to repeal the Insurance Act if his Party managed to get into power. He has had more time than was given to Mr. BONAR LAW to answer that question and he gave a more cautious reply. He would not repeal it, he said, but he would favour an inquiry to see whether it would be possible to have an optional system. An optional system is an impossible system, so that we take it, Mr. SMITH would retain the Insurance Act not- withstanding its alleged imperfections.

Mr. SMITH is very sore because Mr. Burns has refused to lend financial assistance to a scheme for Housing which has been brought forward by the Unionist Social Reform Corn- mittee. In some choice sentences he declared

that people might rot in the hovels of the slums without the Liberal Party caring one jot; and the President of the Local Govern- ment Board, Mr. BURNS, has forgotten all about the slums since he got £5,000 a year. Mr. SMITH conveniently forgot to allude to the fact that against this Unionist scheme there is an established fact—an Act in being. Under the Housing and Town Planning Act, 1909, additional powers have been conferred on local authorities for the purpose of enabling them to deal with insanitary areas and unhealthy dwellings, for facilitating the provision of houses and for bringing under control the development of land in the vicinity of growing centres of popula,- tion with a view not only of securing improve d sanitary conditions but also greater amenity and convenience. Besides, the Old Age Pension Act has reduced indoor paupers over 70 years of age by 95 per cent, and the insurance of the people against times of sickness and the steps taken for the protection of children are a few of the accomplishments which the people may be trusted to remember when these interested attacks are being levelled against statesmen whose only offence is that they have done a record amount of good in the interests of the masses. It was fitting that Mr. SMITH should speak of the " shameless " Minis ters who dealt in American shares. It would have been more fitting had he referred to a really " shameless " act. What about Tariff Reform and food taxes and the " shameless" way in which the question has been shelved in a time of prosperity in order that the party to which Mr. SMITH belongs may traffic on the misfortunes of the country when trade once again becomes bad? On this question he was silent, like Mr. BONAR LAW, like the Warrington Women Tariff Reformers. We shall venture to descibe these tactics as " shameless" and to thank Mr. HAROLD SMITH for teaching us that word.
