div.head: Passing Week.
div.p: The Passing Week.
WELCOME TO THE KING AND QUEEN,

A heart-stirring welcome awaits their' Majesties, the King and Queen, on their visit to our ancient borough on Monday next. The town has already taken upon itself the outward trappings of rejoicing and festivity, and judging from present appearances, the scene in the streets when the finishing touches are completed will be one of splendour and beauty. But of even greater significance than this striking display, will be the spontaneous cheers expressive of the affection in which their Majesties are universally held. By their pattern home life and their genuine interest in the workaday, life of the masses, their Majesties have, in a i remarkably short time, won the regard and admiration of all who have a true conception of the greatness of a nation—that it consists not merely of pomp and power, but in the healthy, happy lives of the toiling multitudes. Warrington is highly honoured in being chosen as the starting place of the Royal tour through Lancashire, and the events of Monday—including as they do, the opening by the King of the first section of the new Warrington Bridge and an inspection of one of the most progressive industrial concerns in the country—will be written large in the long and lustrous history of the town of which we are all so proud.

div.head: RATIONAL HOURS OF LABOUR.
div.p: RATIONAL HOURS OF LABOUR.

Mr. A. H. Crosfield visited Warrington last Saturday to present the trophies won by the successful bowling team in the Peter Peacock Challenge Cup Competition—a remarkably healthy institution—and took advantage of the occasion to refer to the efforts he is making, in conjunction with the International Association for Labour Legisla- tion, for a more rational method of regulating working hours. As we stated last week, Mr. Crosfield has advocated the substitution of an eight-hours day for the old wasteful methods—wasteful in physical, economical and every other sense—in the columns of the " Manchester Guardian," but his speech reported in to-day's " Examiner" will be read with profit by the large number who are interested in the subject. Mr. Crosfield points out in the second of the "Manchester Guardian " articles that the eight-hour shift is making great progress in the iron and steel trade in this country, but the movement is handicapped by the fact that the improved methods are not being applied so readily abroad. That is one of the reasons for the activities of the International Association for Labour Legislation in which Mr. Crosfield is keenly and closely interested. British employers, the "Manchester Guardian" says in an appreciative article, have " the greatest inducement to help forward the inter- national movement, and we hope that Mr. Crosfield's earnest and reasoned appeal for thcir co-operation in this good cause, will meet with a ready and influential response. What is wanted at present is that the Government shoull be encouraged actively to support the Association's policy, if not by taking the lead in calling the proposed inter-
FLAGS, STREAMERS, BUNTING.—J. S. GARLAND, 51' 53, and 55, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt.
national conference, at least by participating in it as an earnest advocate of an agreement to legislate."
ORDER IN VICTORIA PARK

We are glad to note that the Parks Corn- mittee have decided to provide the assistance necessary for the maintenance of order in Victoria Park and that they have asked the Watch Committee to afford special facili- ties for suppressing the disorderly conduct of persons resorting to the Park. It is intoler- able that places which have been set aside for the innocent enjoyment and recreation of the public should be so misused as to make respectable people who wish to use them doubtful of the wisdom of doing so. Perhaps the drastic .steps the Committee evidently contemplate will have the desired effect. May we suggest, while on this subject, that the Committee appear to have done a harsh thing unthinkingly? In railing off a road which may be shut off from the park they have made it necessary for the people cross- ing Howley Bridge to walk into Latchford before they can get into the grounds. A small gate near the river which could be locked at nights would be a great convenience, especi- ally as anyone in future found in the Park after the night bell has been rung is to be summoned before the magistrates.

div.head: PAY FOR SUNDAY LABOUR.
div.p: PAY FOR SUNDAY LABOUR.

The question of paying the tram-men time and a half for Sunday labour was twice before the Committee during the last month and twice adjourned. Evidently to meet the general situation, Councillor Wilson gave notice to move at the Council meeting last Tuesday that all workmen in the employ of the C9rporation required to work on Sunday should be paid at the rate of not less than time and a half. If the matter was to be tackled at all, this, we think, was the way to do it. The principal grievance of the tramway men is that other men in the employ of the Corporation get the extra pay which is denied to them. If the tram-men get the increase, other sections will have their grievance accentuated to that extent. We have heard of men working on the same job on Sunday some of whom received time and a half and some of whom did not because they belonged to another department of the Corpor- ation. A resolution dealing with the matter as a whole, appears to us to be advisable in the interests not only of peace but of fair play. Councillor Wilson's motion was carried, but the Mayor intimated that he should at the next meeting, ask the Council to define the meaning of the word "work- men."

div.head: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

We hope the interest taken in the health of the town by the members of the Council was not fully represented by the attendance at the special meeting called this week to discuss thc annual report of the ex-Medical Officer of Health. There was not a quorum to start with and during the concluding portions of the discussion that did take place not more than a third of the Council were present. The smoke question and the over- crowded condition of certain areas came in for consideration,special attention being given to smoke. There seems to be a sharp division of opinion as to whether certain works in town are exempt from the Acts of Parliament that try to control our chimneys or whether they are only exempt on being able to show that they have used •every endeavour to comply with the needs of the situation. We have some interesting correspondence on the subject to-day.

div.head: MORE HARMFUL THAN SMOKE.
div.p: MORE HARMFUL THAN SMOKE.

Alderman Bennett, ever to the fore in this matter, said something more harmful than smoke was escaping into our atmosphere,kill- ing the trees so surely that he thinks very few will be, left in the Cemetery in a short time. Two months ago, when he made a 'similar statement, Alderman Bolton ridiculed Alderrhan Bennett's assertion and said the trees, which were sending their roots into the sand which underlies the Cemetery, were dying for want of nourishment. "I have been troubled with the same complaint myself," he added, amid loud laughter. Alderman James Evans ventured the opinion that if the new Smoke Abatement Bill had gone through and Local Government Board inspectors had been appointed, they would eliminate the whole of the works of the town in ten years and "substitute that paradise of vegetation that you tell us we ought to see." This is scarcely the way to argue a grave subject. If it is possible to have a healthy atmosphere and the work as well, we ought to have them—and some employers have shown us how the thing may be done.

div.head: AS PIONEER.
div.p: AS PIONEER.

'I have never heard of the Local Govern- ment Board sending a plan back because it was too dear."—Alderman James Evans at the Council, explaining, that the Govern- ment officer had delayd matters in connection with the sanatorium by asking for cheaper plans. Warrington is ever looking to its laurels as a pioneer.

LOCAL WEDDINGS. Winstanley—Long. • The marriage was solemnized at Bewserroad Wesleyan Church on Monday of Mr. Charles Henry • Winstanley, son of Mr. Henry Winstanley, Fern Bank, Manchester-road, and Miss Ethel Long, daughter of Mr. Alfred Long, 34, Pickmere-street. The Rev. W. A. Beckett officiated. The hymns "The voice that breathed o'er Eden," and "0 perfect love" were sung and Mr. T. Tanner, who was at the organ, played Mendelssohn's Wedding March. The bride, who was given away by her father, was beautifully attired in white satin, with hat to match, and carried a lovely bouquet of white roses, carnations and lilies of the valley. The bridesmaids were Miss A. H. Winstanley (sister of the bridegroom) and Miss M. Monks. They wore Saxe blue dresses, with picture hats to match, and their bouquets were composed of white roses and carnations. Their ornaments were gold brooches, the gifts of the bridegroom. Mr. S. F. Reynolds acted as best man. The reception was held at Fern Bank, after which the happy couple departed for Llandudno, where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride travelled in. a grey costume with bat to match.

div.head: RECTOR'S PROTEST.
div.p: RECTOR'S PROTEST.

No Recognition of the Church when the King comes. The Rector (Rev. Canon Willis) has the following comments in the current issue of the Warrington Parish Church Magazine :—Surprise and regret have bees freely expressed at the absence of all recognition of the Church at the approaching visit of the King. The feeling is natural and right. The Church of England is, as all well-instructed Churchpeople know, the one and only true branch of Chtist's Holy Catholic Church in this land. She is also the Established Church officially connected with the State as no other religions body is, and if ever there was an occasion on which her position should have been publicly acknowledged, it is this, when the Head of the State is coming to visit the town. , Some members of the Council have openly expressed their regret at the omission of a very plain duty, and for this they deserve, and we trust they will receive, the thanks of all true Churchmen.

On Monday next, our loyal and ancient town will extend a greeting—typicalon its heartiness and sincerity of the county of Lancaster—to their Majesties King George V. and Queen Mary, who will honour .War- rington by making it the starting point in their motor tour of the County Palatine. There are striking indications on every hand that Warrington will once more rise to the occasion and that the reception accorded to their Majesties here will be such as to invest the day with the happiest recol- lections for the Royal visitors. During the week decorators have been exceedingly busy and the streets are at present in process of transformation. The pillars of the triumphal arches have been placed in position in Arpley-road, at Market Gate, the Town Hall drives and Sankey Bridges; lest Dons of artificial flowers have been hung on the electric standards and the remainder of the official scheme of decoration will be taken in hand this week- end. Meanwhile private enterprise has bestirred itself and most of the shops and places of business are artistically embellished with garlands, bunting and loyal mottoes. Warrington will, indeed, be "Beautiful Warrington" on Monday. Below,we publish, in full, the official programme, issued by the Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph). WALKING DAY.
PIeTURESQUE PAGEFINT.

Children's pag,antry once more held possession f the streets of Warrington iesterday. It was the children's great joy day - known and looked forward to by litt e ones, and by "children of a larger growth " too, as "Walking Day " and the town abandoned itself to holida -making. It is often remarked that each succeeding festival is, in all essentials, a replica of the last, but, be that as it may, every year only serves to enshrine " Walking Day." more securely in the affections of the multitude. They seem to take a special pride in this peculiaev local demonstration which gives Warrington the 'oppor- tunity of enjoying pleasurable relaxation on a day when the whole country has its nose to the grind- stone. Although, on this ccca-ion, the corning of the King and Queen held a commanding place in the thoughts and interest of loyal Warringtonians, it was not allowed to dwarf the festival to any noticeable extent, and, as in previous years, the sole c,tric,>rn of all and sundry was to enable the scholars to have a right joyous time. A FESTAL SETIING. The preparations fur the I-loyal vi-it pave the pro- cession a brighter setting than usual, fur toe main streets were ablaze with flags, garlands and festoons, which imparted a happy finishing touch to scenes of colour and animation. After several deys of almostunbroken sunshine, the weather conditions moon- sider:tely fell far short cf tlge ideal yesterday when so much was hoped of them. The morning dawned with lowering skies, a falling barometer and a nipping air. Anxious glances were directed skyward, and, when drizzling rain threatened, the hopes of all, except the children—whose spirits are quite unconquerable—fell almost to zero. Happily, however, the processions were carried out without the necessity to resort to umbrellas, but the absence of radiant sunshine detracted somewhat from the brilliance of the picture. During the afternoon, when the scholars had repaired to fields in the locality, there was a return of the rain, and the sports programmes were gone through under difficulties.

THE SCENE AT THE TOWN HALL. It was on the lawn in front of the Town Hall that the most impressive spectacle of the day was witnessed. Here the scholars of the Church of England and several Nonconformist and undenominational schools massed in their thousands until the greensward was practically covered. From the Royal pavilion, which will be the scene of the civic welcome to the King and Queen, the Mayor and Mayoress and other pro- minent townspeople viewed the muster. Lord Derby, who had come to give his final approval to the rangements for their Majesties' visit,appeared on the scene just as the schools were taking up their posi- tions and was, for a few moments an interested spectator. The dominant impression, just before the procession began to move through the centre arch, was of a mass of white, with here and there splashes of nicely' harmonising colours, and a perfect forest of handsome banners. The eye of the onlooker was charmed, hut to the ear the effect was somewhat mixed. From all quarters came bands, blaring forth with deligltful ineependence,and the selections—heard at one and the same time—ranged from sombre hymn tunes to sprightly marches and popular ditties. It was, however, the bandsman's harvest day and they were forgiven much. It was nearly ten minutes after the appointed time ten o'clock—when the gates were opened, and the Blue Coat School led the way in the march through the town. The order of the procession was as follow: 1. Blue Coat School and Band. 2. Padgate Cottage Homes and Band. 3. Fait field and Crosfield's Band. 4. National. 5. St. George's and Grappenhall Band. G. St. Clement's. 7. St. Peter's and Cheshire Lines Band. S. St. James' and Territorial Band. 9. St. Ann's and Penketh Tannery Band. 10. St. Paul's and Church Lads' Brigade Band. 11. All Saints' and Ardwick Green Industrial Band. 32. Holy Trinity and Walton Band. 13. Factory Yard Mission. 14. St. Luke's. 15. St: Barnabasi and Preston Brook Band. 16. Emmanuel. 17. Buckley-street and the Pioneer Band. 15. Brick-street and Friars' Green. 19. Salvation Army and Band. 20 Ragged School and Drum and Fife Band. PRETTY FEATURES OF A GREAT PROCESSION.

The procession is always chiefly impressive as a demonstration of numerical strength, but on this occasion, it had an outstanding claim to spectacular beauty. Quite a number of schools had put forth specidl efforts to introduce daintily contrived novelties which relieved the display from anything approaching monotony. St. Peter's school maintained its reputa- tion in this direction. Groups of little Red Riding Hoods were attired after the approved fashion of the nursery tale ; Australian girls cracked their whips, as if to give the impression that they were fearless horsewomen ; and flower girls carried baskets of choice blooms. St. George's Mission and St. Luke's school were notable for an array of garlands and floral arches, while All Saints' Mission had a dignified little May Queen and retinue. Companies of the Church Lads' Brigade paraded with several of the Church schools, and their smart appearance and soldierly bearing were the subject of much favourable comment. Buckley-street school is to be credited with the display comprising the most varied and original features. A. bevy of fascinating fairies carried silvery wands, Quakeresses did their utmost to look demeure, and Japanese maids tripped blithely along. The Mission workers followed the excellent precedent which they established a few years ago, of making a collection on behalf of the "Children of War- rington Cot" at the Warrington Infirmary. Point was given to the appeal by a realistic tableau, representing a cot, with a patient in charge of nurses Great admiration was aroused by a troupe of Morris dancers, who went through their old-time measure in happy and natural style. The Salvation Army and the Ragged School always mark the occasion by an effort to shed brightness into otherwise cheerless lives, and the poor children whom they were entertaining for the day looked smiling and cheerful, in spite of straitened circumstances. _ _ _
The procession was marshalled by Mr. P. T. Fairclough and Mr. Lionel Fairclough. The police arrangements, under the control of the Chief Constable (Mr. M. Nichols), were admirable in every detail.
The Great ehildren's Festival unmarred by Threatening Skies.

PARISH. CHURCH PROCESSION. and quiet dignity. Each s-hool had its distinctive colour scheme. Litt e children, in white suits and diessts, with sashes and caps of delicate colours, earl ied choice bouquets or garlands. The lavish display of lilies was something to marvel at. The children marched with military precision, obedient to the directions of their teachers, and whenever there was a momentary halt one could hear the huh, feet marking time. We thought the loveliest feature of the whole pageant %.as the pure wh;te statue of the Madonna and Child, which formed part of St. Mary's procession. It was carried beneath a canopy of lilies and greenery, from which bung sti earners of smil ix and riboon, borne by girls whose hair was covered with floral wreaths. There were several other beautifully decorated statues, as well as almost innumerable floral devices. The Gaelic pipers from St. Joseph's Industrial School, Longsigtit, made a brave show in their old Hibernian costumes, their green standard proudly held aloft. Tney were repeatedly applauded by the crowds who lined the route. The Boys' Brigade movement has spread to the Roman Catholic Church aril a strong contingent from tSt. Mary's Church bore themselves well and were admirably disciplined. The procession was in every respect worthy of the best traditions of the Roman Catholic processions in Warrington - the highest tribute that could be paid to it.
THE NONCONFORMIST SCHOOLS.

Most of the Nonconformist schools betook them- selves direct to rural resorts. with the object of givina the children a whole day in the fields. Wycliffe School journeyed to Dunham Hill; Bold-street Wesleyans and Golborne-street Baptists to Acton Bridge; Cairo-street I.lbitarians and Legh-street Primitive Methodists to Lymm ; and Silver-street and Ellesmere-street Wesleyans to Helsby.

div.head: ROMAN CATHOLIC PAGEANT.
div.p: THE ROMAN CATHOLIC PAGEANT.

No one would venture to dispute that the Roman Catholics invariably carry off the palm for the exquisite beauty of their pageantry. That love of the ornate and symbolic which characteris.,s their religious observances finds striking expression on this occasion, and produces a display which is highly impressive, as well as picturesque. No more pleasing procession has been seen in Warrington than that which traversed the streets yesterday. There was uniformity amid vat iety, artistic grouping, a wealth of floral embellish- ment and, crowning all, an atmosphere of stateliness

div.head: ALL ABOUT THE SCHOOLS
div.p: ALL ABOUT THE SCHOOLS
Features of the Procession and How the Day was Spent. SPECIAL RETURNS TO THE "EXAMINER."
We have obtained the following returns from the various schools as to their numerical streogth,features of the procession, and how the day was spent :

div.head: CHURCH OF ENGLAND.
div.p: CHURCH OF ENGLAND.

NATIONAL (Bors).—The scholars met at the schools at nine and joined the procession round the townoilong with the other parochial schools. Afterwards a service wag held at the Parish Church, the preacher being the Rev. T. T. Lee Jones, Vicar of Daresbury. By kind permission of the Principal of the Training College,the field in Salisbury-street was placed at the disposal of the scholars for the usual sports. Crostield's band, which headed the procession, played selections through- out the day. Tea was provided, a tent having been erected for the purpose. div.head: DROWNING FATALITY Casts Gloom Over Walking Day Treat. FATAL ATTEMPT AT RESCUE.
div.p: DROWNING FATALITY Casts Gloom Over Walking Day Treat. FATAL ATTEMPT AT RESCUE.

A gloom was cast over the Walking Day treat in connection with St. Paul's School by a drowning fatality, a former scholar named Henry Johnson, aged twelve, son of James Johnson, fireman, 16, Edgeworth- street, being drowned in an attempt to rescue a com- panion named Thomas Welsby, of Mill-lane, who had fallen into the St. Helens and Sankey Canal at Bewsev. The lads were playing in the neighbourhood of Johnson's house, but suddenly disappeared, and Johnson's parents heard nothing more of him until be was brought home dead. It appears that at two o'clock the boys went for a walk nen' Bewsey Park, where St. Paul's school children were holding their festival. They were going along the canal bank and, in throwing a stone into the water, Welsby slipped and fell in. Johnson leaned over the bank and held out his hand, which Welsby grasped. The result was that Johnson lost his balance and was immersed. Welsby was able to regain the bank, but Johnson sank. An alarm was raised and the body was recovered by Mr. Eastwood, of Bewsey Lodge Artificial respiration was tried for twenty minutes by Acting-Sergeant Newey, but without success. The body was taken home by the members of the St. Paul's Church Lads' Brigade. The teachers of St. Paul's School have asked the Rev. W. Bracecamp to express their sympathy with the bereaved relatives.

div.head: GIRL INJURED BY TAXI.
div.p: GIRL INJURED BY TAXI.

Annie Smutcb, aged 11 years, 33, Oxford-street, was knocked down in Knutsford-road last night by a Lion Hotel taxi-cab. She was taken to the Infirmary where it was found that her head was severely injured and her condition early this morning was very cirical.

div.head: ALEXANDRA DAY.
div.p: ALEXANDRA DAY.
Some Reminiscences by a Lady Rose Seller. TOUCHING HEARTS AND POCKETS.

Warrington kept Alexandra Day on Satur- day, and the celebrations were a magnificent success. The gross pro- ceeds amount to £482 us. 10d.. of which sum £421 Bs. Id. was derived from the sale of flowers.

Alexandra Day The sun shone brightly on gay 'ladies who, in their prettiest of snow-white dresses and baskets of wild roses, decked the sombre streets of our town on Saturday last. Alexandra Day The idea of its beauty and usefulness was over all. The people talked "Alexandra Day," the streets looked "Alexandra Day," the very air was filled with "Alexandra Day"; and later the sun beams, ashamed to bide themselves under clouds, as they wished to do, sent forth their gladdening rays for Alexandra Day: Strangers who came into the town felt the benefic'ent effects of Alexandra Day and entered into the spirit of it with zest, so, that the Infirm- ary. will, with gratefulness, remember its bene- factors. At noon almost every person had a tiny token of the Queen-Mother, and empty baskets showed that trade had been brisk, suave voices had been busy, hearts touched and hands been deep in pockets.

There were a few incidents which helped to relieve the tedium of the day and made one forget for the time one's tired limbs. Some of the soldiers from the Barracks declined to buy a rose because they were not allowed to wear flowers on their\uniforrus, but they soon found out that it was better to brave Guard Room or Captain's wrath rather than give pain to the ladies. I hope the Captain was. merciful. I offered once to plead on "Tommy's" behalf, but as he was much taller than I am, and looked "down" on me, I expect lie thought it wasn't worth while. Detective Metcalfe also said the Chief would object to "more than one," but eventually he invested in a rose for his confrere, and the latter returned the com- pliment gracefully. When they were going away they gave me a parting shot : "If the ,Chief cuts up rough—" I interrupted: "Introduce him to me." So perhaps I may be called upon later for the interview. I am quite ready and not a bit afraid. Forewarned is forearmed Mr. Nicholls ! !

There were many people who had no change, but then the ladies were ever ready to oblige, and managed to get the sovereigns changed every time. Then the men paid up with a smile. Some of them would insist on the ladies pinning the roses on their caps, and then ask : "Does it look nice?" I wonder if ever you heard that men were not vain? Vanitas vanitatum amnia vani- tas. One of the men when I asked would be h have one for his cap answered me with : "Do you think I'm a blooming horseparader?" He had passed on before I recovered from my amaze- ment.

Another gentleman in quite a businesslike tone, when asked to buy, said,: "Certainly I will, for you see buying a rose is a twofold benefit—it benefits the Infirmary and benefits the flower- makers." Something which I endorsed quite readily. Another member of the sterner sex who walked about town with an observant eye ventured a remark to my companion thus : "You seem to have all the Suffrage Society working to-day." A remark which was very near the truths. _

All the artifices of the sellers were taxed to the utmost. I remember asking one old gentleman. who persistently refused to provide a mate for his solitary blossom, "to buy one for his walking stick then," and he went off down the street, in such a fit of hilarious laughter that he couldn't restrain himself ,from coming back a nioment later to show me the disastrous effects of my pleading. "See. what I've done; ire burst my collar 1"

"Hello!' said my companion, interrupting a brisk moment .of trade, "Here's Florrie Forde," and I moved towards her offering her my roses. "Why, I've only just .finished selling myself," she answered, "but I'll certainly have a bunch from you when I come back." About an hour later the popular artiste, accompanied by a charming doggie on leash, came back to patronise my rose tray with a "You see I didn't forget." Then the frolicsome, poodle clamoured for my attention, by pawing my dress. I addrested him in French, when to my surprise' his mistress broke out with a surprised exclamation in that same language. I was rather taken aback, and then in the anim- ated chat which followed she told me she had been to school in France. I shall always look back upon the little interview with pleasure. Her "Au Revoir Madame, et bonne chance," uttered in quite a soft, sweet tone, still rings in my ears, and I don't think I shall ever forget it. ' A doctor, well known in town; told Me that he had asked one young lady 'a question in reply to the usual demand, which was as follows : "Do you imagine that I'm a, May Queen?" He forgot to give me her answer, but as he was nicely de- corated we can surmise the result. For Alexan- dra Day the worthy doctor would even risk being taken for a May Queen! 1 Bravo, doctor ! !

Another, little- incident caused me much merri- ment—since. When I asked one young gentle- man to invest in a flower because he hadn't any tie quite gracefully said "No, thank you," and raised his hat so that I could see inside, and : He wore a wreath of roses Inside the crown of his hat." How he smiled when I saw them 1!
Later in the afternoon I espied our Member coming down the street, and our conversation was somewhat as follows : "Another rose, Mr. Smith?" His answer and manner somewhat startled me.

"Look here, 420 ladies have asked me to-day." "Well, that must indeed have been pleasant." "Oh ! there's a limit, even to pleasant things." "I don't think so," said I. "One can't have too much of a good thing," and it very quickly flashed across my mind how many times I had heard that Mi. H. Smith was pleased .to repre- sent Warrington, and I'm sure that if an election were drawing near he would not desire any limita- tion to that pleasant thing. Then he continued : "I have already spent 305." and whilst he put a coin into my box I very nearly retorted with something about £4OO a year and Warrington, but I refrained, so he added :

"I'll take good care I keep out of 'Warrington next Alexandra Day." That was indeed too much for me, and I answered not a word, so to change the subject he asked if we felt cold, and as we answered in the negative he said : "I hope you won't take cold," then raised his hat and went away. For a short time the joy of Alexan- dra Day seemed clouded, but shortly afterwards under the genial influence of the roses I entered heartily _ into business once more. _ _
Towards the close of evening work a ragged newspaper boy who was close by looked wistfully up at me and with a sunny smile, but in a sym- pathetic tone said : "You haven't sold out yet, Miss."

"No, neither have you, laddie," I replied, re- turning his smile, and he looked down at his bundle of papers; but very soon we wished him "good-night and good luck" and we trudged off with our boxes and trays to • the Infirmary. On coming out we met Mr. T. Broadbent going in with his arms filled with money boxes, evidently brought from Latchford, whilst • his sister kept guard over many more in the car._
- Then my companion and I, feeling dreadfully tired, with sore throats, aching limbs, but con- tented hearts, wended our way homeward in the waning light.

div.head: Cottage Fire.
div.p: Cottage Fire.

At ten o'clock last nigl; a fire broke nut at the residence of Albert Forster, 13. Old-road, Warrington. The Fire brigade under Supt. Turner were quickly on the spot and succeeded in putting the fire out.

div.head: COUNTRYSIDE
div.p: THE COUNTRYSIDE
Value of a Love for Open-Air Pursuits and interests.

AGE HOLDS irs OWN WITH YOUTIf It is quite exhilarating to see my friend "Silver Street" writing so enthusiastically in his cylists' note book of the young men of sixty and seventy years of age who still keep up their practical fondness for the wheel. There is nothing more conducive to a hearty, healthy, and lively enjoy- ment of a vigorous old age than a love of open-air pursuits of various kinds. Many instances have come under my notice of late, which, whilst not requiring so much purely animal strength and physical endurance as a cross-country cycle tide, are nevertheless very suggestive that a man is just as young and no older than he feels. The golf course and the bowling green have both been claimed as the particular domains .of old men, and no doubt these claim a goodly portion, but there is still a large percentage who find their recreation in other ways. Gardening, walking, and botanising all have their quota, and here age can hold its own with, youth. The prizes and the championships are not -monopolised by those un- der forty.

Young Octogenarians. I was reminded of this at last summer's Flower Show at Frodsham, where a hale and hearty young cottage gardener of eighty walked away with nearly all the first prizes in the show. Com- ing nearer home, the wild flower table at the Museum owes a very large part of its success during the last five years to three young men whose total ages amount to two hundred and ten years. As a collector, Mr. Fred Fuller con- tributed every year over eight hundred specimens of wild flowers. This young man went to New Zealand two years ago to begin life again at the age of sixty. He is prospering well in the colony, and quite likely to last for another sixty years. Ralph Burrows, of Grappenhall, who died three weeks ago, was another of the Museum's young men. As regular as the clock, every Wednesday afternoon at two o'clock Mr. Burrows brought in his big bunch of flowers. They were specially appreciated and valuable, because they were carefully selected. No one knew the flora of Grappenhall, and the country- side between it and Great Budworth better than he did. He took long walks both on Sunday after morning church and after he finished his day's work in seeking choice flowers for the Museum table. He always knew, almost to the day, when the various species first appeared in bloom, and all the "early spots" were known to him. When he died it 70 years of age the countryside lost •a real lover who loved it for its own sake. Many of the rarer plants of his neighbourhood he never touched, loving rather to watch them grow and spread. The only time I ever saw him angry .was one day when he came to report that some unknown vandal had taken a rare plant up by the root. The Museum local herbarium contains many "good things which he went miles specially to procure. Another young man comes frequently en market days from Earlestown. He is only eighty years old as yet, and has only been•interested in botany for a few years. I get ene of the treats of my working week when my young friend comes in with "a few things which I have picked this morning on the railway and on the Common." The "few. things" very often is equivalent to forty or fifty different species. When the "fest- things" are unwrapped and untied it is my pleasure to go over them individually with our friend, and if he knows he names the flowers as they come; if he doesn't, I help. Then we adjourn to the flower- table and go over the plants there one by one, with a few remarks about each. In this way the time passes quickly, and then at the end of the talk my friend, as he, shakes my hand, says: "Well, I'm. getting to know some on 'em; in another ten years or so I think I'll know the most on 'em 1"

Young Ladies of Seventy. "Silver Street:' made one great omission. He did not, I noticed, make any reference to young ladies of :sixty or seventy. I wonder why? Was it because there are no "old" ladies nowadays? Perhaps I ni4 be allowed to correct the slip by referring- to "just one." have the privilege and pleasure to belong to a Garden Society in the neighbourhood, which has a very large Junior Section. Every month the Juniors,- whose ages range from ten to sixteen years, have a country ramble. The. most regular attender of these out- ings is a young lady of seventy-six, who has not missed a ramble for, two years. or her years she is wonderful, and finishes at the end of the afternoon fresher than many of the "older" folks present. Now "Silver Street" I don't think your cyclists can beat us mere pedestrians and botanists for a perennial youth

The Delights of Botany. I know of no more delightful hobby than that of field botany. By this is not meant wild flower gathering or collecting. Many of the best botan- ists I know hardly ever pluck a flower in the field, except perhaps, now and then, a critical species for purposes of study. Personally I do not, nor ever have collected wild flowers except for Museum purposes. To be a botanist, collect- ing is not necessary. The flowers can be best studied in their special habitats, soils and sea- sons. No great expensive outfit is necessary, not even a bicycle! All that is needed •is a book, like Hayward's "Botanist's Pocket Manual," a note book and pencil, and what a botanist friend of mine expressively calls a pair of "hygroscopic" boots. Anyone who has attempted to study the flora of a bog, like that at Hatchmere, will ap- preciate the humour hidden in the word. An entomologist can scarcely help becoming a collec- tor, owing to the mobility of his objects of study, but flowers have the advantage that they are stationary and do not run or fly away out of reach. The sporting element is lost perhaps, but other elements are added. One of the commonest objections to botany as a hobby is, I believe, the tradition that it is necessary to learn a "heathen language" before one can make much headway. This is a greatly mistaken notion, and has arisen very largely from the way‘ in which the subject is, or was until recently, taught in the schools. Botany is a stiff subject to read up for an ex- amination, especially as often happens in the winter when no lkve specimens can be obtained for study, but to study the flowers growing by the wayside, in the field, on the moor, and up the mountain is as delightful a pastime as one could wish to find. One very quickly makes the ' acquaintance of the commoner flowers and learns to know them by name. Soon after, the mind, almost unconsciously, begins to divide them into groups or families, or to use the scientific term, into "natural orders." The real value of botanis- ina then begins to be apparent, for the powers of observation are coming into active operation and a thousand and one-odd facts which formerly seemed to have no connection with each other are now falling into their natural relationship and co-relationship. We begin to notice the in- fluence of the special nature of the various soils on the plant life. We learn for instance that the meadowlands have a special group ~of plants of their own which are not found in marshy land; that maritime plants are not found inland, and that mountain plants are absent in the valleys. We note, too, the effect of climate, of competition between the various plant associations, of man's interference, and many other phases of plant economy. As we advance in our knowledge of the vegetable kingdom, we begin to ask the how, why and wherefore of things; and the study of the higher branches of botany becomes as fascinating as- the more elementary. Such questions as the origin Of the land flora of Great Britain, the migration of plants, the plant records in the rocks, all speak of an almost inexhaustable storehouse. All the time our observation in the field has been doubtless coupled with many links of associative reading, and it is possible that before proceeding very far we felt the need cf a text book to explain the v rious forms and structures of plants. The dry. te -1, t book with its morphology when studied in the natural place—in the field—becomes quite a different-book from what it is in the class-room. Whatever it may mean to the teacher, a little morphology goes a long way with the field botanist.
There is no hobby like it for training the observation, keeping the body supple and fit with abundant exercise, the eye keen, the mind fresh and well stored, and the spirit young.
G. A. 'DUNLOP.
GARDEN FURNITURE, TENTS, HAMMOCKS, CHAIRS, &c.—J. S. GARLAND, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge et,,. Warrington.—Advt.

div.p: COUNCIL AND SUNDAY TRADING.
The Mayor Asked to Reassure Shopkeepers who are Alarmed by Police Notice.

div.head: WARRINGTON BRIDGE CONTENTIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BRIDGE CONTENTIONS.

Although the agenda for the meeting of the 'Warrington Town Council did not contain many apparently contentious proposals, the proceedings were more than usually protracted. The Council met an hour earlier than usual to discuss the annual report of the Medical Officer, and it was not until 8.40 that all the business was disposed of. One of the most interesting topics touched upon was the action of the police with regard to Sunday trading. The Mayor was invited to reassure small shopkeepers, who are feeling alarmed at the posibility of Police Court proceedings, but his Worship was unable to state definitely whether prosecutions are contemplated or not. The question t.f payment for Sunday labour again engaged attention, and the Council passed a rt-solution ttiat "all workmen in the employ of the Corporation, required by the conditions of their employment to undertake Sunday work, be paid at the rate of not less than time and a half for such work." There was considerable discussion as to the scope of the resolution, and the Mayor intimated that at the next meeting of the Town Council he would bring forward a resolution defining the term "work- man." Questions relating to the ornamentation of Warrington Bridge gave rise to contention, the griev- ance being that, on the authority of the Bridges Committee, work had been put in hand without the necessary confirmation by the Council.
SUNDAY TRADING.
SHOPKEEPERS NERVOUS AT POLICE ACTION.
WILL THERE BE PROSECUTIONS?

On tbe minutes of the Watch Committee being submitted, Councillor PEACOCK invited a statement from the Mayor with reference to the possibility or otherwise of prosecutions in Warrington for Sunday trading. He stated that he had had complaints about the serious inconvenience and annoyance to which shop- keepers had been put through police officers visiting their shops regarding Sunday closing. At the last meeting of the Genral Purposes Committee it was generally understood that the Council were not going any further in the matter, or, at any rate, were not going to risk the fiascos which had taken place at Southport, York "and other ridiculous places." He would like the public and those small shopkeepers who were suffering from nervous attacks, caused by the police visits, to be reassured by an official statement from the Mayor. There were some widows and poor people who were dependent upon their Sunday takings who could not sleep for the thoughts of the policemen going round. Only last week officers visited some of the shops, and yet last Monday the General Purposes Committee almost unanimously decided that nothing further should he done or said. He agreed that some of the shopkeepers ought to close ou Sunday, but they could not enforce it as a general rule without punishing -others who were deserving. The MAYOR replied that although the matter was ont of order he might explain that the question had been raised by an influential deputation waiting upon the Vetch Committee. The police wero directed to make inquiries and report upon the number of shops open on Sundays. The visits had been made with the object of obtaining particulars for the report, and not with the object of taking prosecutions up to the present. Of course he was not in a position to say how the -question would be treated eventually by prosecution or otherwise.
Councillor GOUGH asked whether it was the inten- tion of the Watch Committee to spend money in prose- cutions ithout ths sanctir,n of the Council.

The NlAroft: I think I have given a sufficient and an explicit answer on the question as far as I can at this stage. The committee have given no instructions for prosecutions. The report was requested in response to a large deputation, who waited upon the Watch Com- mittee, and nothing further than the police obtaining the report which has been submitted to the Watch Committee has been done. I am not in a position to say whether anvthing further will be done. Councillor GOUGH : I should like to ask whether be Watch committee can spend money on proceedings ithis kind without the Council's sanction.

The MAYOR: You must give notice of that question. It is all out of order. I have merely answered Coun- cillor Peacock as a matter of courtesy. Councillor ROBERTS deprecated a discussion on the general question while the matter was sub judice. Councillor PEMBERTON having expressed dissatisfac- tion with the course which the police were adopting, the matter was allowed to drop.
at a cheaper rate than the Gas Committee could supply the means of illumination. The MAYOR : This is not on the minutes. THE MOTOR 'BUSES.

On the minutes of the Electricity Committee being submitted, Councillor LASHFORD asked whether it was correct that inexperienced men were being allowed to drive the motor 'buses? He had been told that the men who were at present doing the work had to be instructed by experienced drivers. Councillor PEMBERTON said some of the experienced tram drivers felt it a grievance that outniders had been imported to drive the 'buses. The committee ought to have given their old servants an opportunity of doing the work.

Councillor PEACOCK pointed out the difficulty of a tram driver accommodating hin self to the driving of a motor 'bus. The committee would have preferred to employ their own drivers if they could have felt safe, and it was their intention, when two or three men had got thoroughly accustomed to the work, to fill up vacancies from their own i department. The MAYOR thought it was much better for a man to undertake such driving anew, without any preconceived ideas.
Alderman SMETHURST said the committee had taken every precaution to guard against accident.
THE BRIDGE. WHY NOT CALL ll' KING'S BRIDGE?

Alderman SMETHURST, in submitting the minutes of the Bridges Committee, expressed satisfaction at the honour which was about to ae done to the town by the opening of the first portion of the bridge by tbe King. The MAYOR, referring to the dicision of the Bridges Committee, to call the bridge " iVarrington Bridge," said he was sorry they could not name it " King's Bridge." It seemed superfluous to say it was Warring- ton Bridge, when everyone knew it was in thelborough. Alderman TINNION : It is the Warrington Bridge. Councillor BROADHURST reLrred to a paragraph recommending the provision of an inscription plate, costing 37i guineas, to be fixed on the bridge, com- memorating the opening by the King. The plate was to bear an inscription and the comes of Councillor Joseph as mayor, Alderman Smethurst as the chairman of the Bridgea Committee, and Mr. J. J. Webster as engineer. He urged that the work which had been done by Aldermn Forshaw during his mayoralty in getting the Bill for the building of the bridge through Parliament should be recognised by including the Alderman's name in the inscription. The MAYOR : 1 believe the plate is made. COtHaefflOr BROADHURST : I strongly object to the action of the engineer in having a plate made before he has obtained the sanction of the Council. The MAYOR : He obtained the sanction of the committee. Councillor PEMBERTON said the Council seemed to be getting into a lax way in regard to spending money before the Council had snnctioned it. The MAYOR observed that when the whole bridge was completed another tablet would be placed on tho structure and that would be the proper time for Alder- man For:how's name to be included in any inscription which might be decided upon. AHernian BENNETT urged that the history of the bridge should be recorded on cemmemorative tablets. During the discussion,Councillor BROADHURST asked permission to reply to a remark by Couucillor Lashford The MAyort : Tell him quietly. Councillor BROADHURST : Yes, I will. The MAYOR : Tell him when you see him n outside. Councillor BROA.DHURST : I don't sell ale, if he does, for a living. _ _

On being called to order by the Mayor, Councillor Broadhurst withdrew the remark. Alderman FORSHAW said he had no idea that the subject was to be brought forward and he certainly did not press it. At the same time he was sure every member of the Council desired to give credit to whom credit was due.

At a meeting of the Bridges Committee, a letter was read from the engineer pressing the Committee to agree to the fixing of the mooring rings on the completed portion of the Bridge, in accordance with his design, at an estimated cost for the four rings of .£5O. It was resolved that the engineer be authorised to fix the rings subject to his obtaining a tender for the work and the cost not exceeding the amount named. Later the ENGINEER reportel that the cost of the rings would be 473 guineas. Aldermen TINNION moved an amendment that the minute be referred back. He said the proposal to pur- chahe the rings had been discussed on many occasions' and the committee had been against it. He believed that, instead of the rings being an ornament to the bridge, they would be an eyesore—and' that impression was strengthened by the appearance of similar rings on Westminster Bridge, London. The expenditure had been pushed down their throats, like many other things in connection with the bridge. it was time the Council said "No."

In reply to Councillor Hawthorn, the MAYOR said the rings already been made. Councillor LINDLEY seconded the amendment. On each previous occasion when the proposal to buy the rings bad been brought forward it had met with emphatic refusal. Now it had been got through at a small meeting. The expenditure was unnecessary and would not add to the beauty of the bridge. Councillor OsnoRNE said a protest ought to be made against work being proceeded with before it had received the sanction of the Council. To refer the minute back at this stage, would be no satisfaction, if the expense had been incurred. At the same time, they would not like the bridge to be spoiled, after spending so much on it.
The MAYOR said I e was satisfied, from what the engineer had told him, that the rings would be no disfigurement.
Alderman SMETITURST said the rings on Westminster Bridge were an ornament..

COUDCIIIOr BIRTLES maintained that the rings would enhance the appearance of the bridge. Councillor LASIIFORD : Whatever the engineer suggests, CounclPor Birtles is always with him. The MA Yoit : That is a personal remark. Councillor BIRTLES : I must ask for it to be with- drawn.
The MAYOR : It is certainly not a proper remark. It is implying that Councillor Birtles is a partisan of Mr. Webster.

Councillor LASIIFORD : What I said is perfectly true. I would not siy it, if it were not true. The MA.vott : These personal remarks lead to no end of trouble, and I am not going to allow them. You roust either withdraw the remark or resume your seat. Take the option. Councillor BROADHURST : Withdraw it. I have done. (Laughter.) Councillor BIRTLE : It takes a gentleman to with- draw anything. The MAYOR (to Councillor Lashford): You must either withdraw the remark or resume your seat. Councillor Lashford : If I were in fault, I would withdraw it. (The Councillor then resumed his seat.) Councillor ROBERTS pointed out that the Bridges Committee consisted of the whole of the members of the Council, and if those who were not present at the meeting in question were desirous of being fair to those who were, they ought to allow the resolution to pass. Councillnr PEMBERTON supported the amendment. He said the matter might seem a small one, but it was improper thatfit should be thrust down their throats. Alderman BENNKTT said the Council would waste half-an-hour in discussing a trivial matter, but when a report affecting the lives and health of 70.000 people came up for consideration there was barely a quorum, Councillor DicKiNsoN opposed the purchase on principle. How many extras had the Council over- looked already ? The engineer actually sent a letter to the Bridges Committee offering to give .£lO towards the cost of these lions heads. It was an insult to the Bridges Committee to make such an offer. The amendment was lost by 13 votes to 9. SUNDAY LABOUR. ' HALF FOR MEN.

div.head: TRADE UNION'S SUCCESSFUL PLEA.
div.p: TRADE UNION'S SUCCESSFUL PLEA.

Alderman TINNION, in submitting the minutes of the Paving and Sewerage Committee, which were adopted, stated that the Committee had received a deputaeion from the Amalgamated Operative Street Masons, Pay iota and Stoneoresserg' Society with reference to a request for an increase of wages to paviors. They met in a friendly spirit, and he believed the increases subse- quently passed by the committee would give entire Latisfactioo.

The minutes showed that increases varying from 2s. to 33. per week were granted to 17 employee, including pavrors, rarnmers, stonemasons and labourers. It was also recorded that two of the contractors for carting attended and requested the committee to make an increase in their contract prices on account of the increases of wages. The committee informed the con- acters that they could not vary the contract. LADIES AND BOWLING GREENS.

Councillor OSBORNE said that at the last meeting of the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee it was decided to set apart all the municipal bowling greens for the use of ladies from 2 to 5.30 p.m. on Tuesdays. He noticed that the decision did not appear on the minutes, and would he be right in assuming that the greens would be thrown open in the way suggested next week ? Ho also wished to know whether the ladies could be prevented from using the greens at any time? Alderman TINIsIION : You cannot prevent them at all. They might go on at midnight and spoil them. (Laughter.) Councillor OSBORNE : If we don't prevent the ladies going on, can we prevent the men from using the greens on Tuesday afternoons ? Councillor BROADHURST asked the committee to expedite the opening of the green in Liverpool-road to ladies on Tuesday. Councillor DICKENSON said the question would come before the committee at a later stage. Personally he was opposed to the proposal which had been made that ladies should have, the exclusive use of the greens on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons.
THE GAS PROFITS. GOOD NEWS FOR CONSUMERS.

Councillor OSBORNE drew attention to the report issued by the Nlanager of the Gas Works, which stated that 1912 bad been the most prosperous year exoerienced. The time was therefore opportune to consider the claims of the consumers. He pointed out that the last reduction in the price of gas was made on November Ist, 1909, and he asked whether something could not be done still further to reduce the price to consumers. Alderman JOHN EVANS stated that the committee were now considering the question of a reduction, but it was not a matter of wnether the price should be reduced, but how much it was to be reduced.

Councillor OsßoßNic next pointed out that the report stated that, although the net receipts were £2,000 less than last year's, the past year was the most prosperous one experienced. He (the councillor) thought there must be some mistake, for, as far as he could see, the receipts were not £2,000 less but £7,560 more. Probably the mistake had arisen through the altered form in which the accounts were made out. If members would refer to the previous year's statement they would find that discounts and reserves were not deducted from the gross receipts, as in the present accounts, and it was quite evident that the net amount this year was com- pared with the gross amount of last year. He hoped that the committee would see their way to concede as large a reduction as possible to those people who, at the present time, were paying to reduce the rates of people who were not using the gas. Councillor PEMBERTON hoped the committee would cot repeat the mistake made on the previous occasion, when they forgot the slot meter users. Alderman TINNION said the slot meter users were not forgotten ; it was a matter of readjusting the meters. Councillor PEAT BERTON : The slot meter users have not always received the same reductions as the other consumers have. Councillor Got-c fr said that if reductions were to be made the price ought to be fixed on a just and equit- able basis all round. The ordinary consumers got is liberal discount, but the slot meter users got no dis- count whatever. The poorest people—those who could least afford to pay—had to pay more than the ordinary consumers.

Councillor BROADH URST said there were firms in this town who were receiving thousands of pounds of benefits from the gas undertaking without contributing a single farthing to its success. The committee were, therefore, to be complimented upon the course they were taking in finding out whether it would be more beneficial to devote the profits to reducing the price rather than to the relief of rates. Alderman JOHN EvANs said the claims of the slot meter users had always been recognised, but it was diflicult to readjust the meters all at the same time. Councillor ROBERTS, referring to the second point raised by Councillor Osborne, said the statement in the report was quite correct. The net results of the manu- facture of gas, as such, were £2,000 worse than last year. At a later stage, COUtiCillOr BROADHURST sskedfif the Llectricity Committee could not adopt" out-throat competition," and supply current for slot meters, even,

div.head: TIME AND A HALF FOR CORPORATION WORK-
div.p: TIME AND A HALF FOR CORPORATION WORK-

Councillor WILSON moved : "That all workmen in the employ of the Corporation required by the condi- tions of their employment to undertake Sunday work be paid at a rate of not less than time and a half for such work, and that this resolution come into operation on and after the Ist August, 1913." Councillor PEACOCK seconded.

Councillor BROADIT t'II,ST supported, and said the movement suggested by the resolution was taking place throughout the country. Corporations were now adopting not only time and a half on Sundays but time s,nd a quarter for all overtime. So far its his knowledge went, all trade unionists would be in favour of the resolution.

Alderman TINNION said the matter was being con- sidered by the various committees of the Corporation, and it was not right to take it out of their hands. This was one of those sweeping, drastic resolutions that applied justly and unjustly. There were men whose conditions of labour were such that their Sunday work had already been taken into consideration in fixing their wages. The resolution as at present drafteol would apply to caretakers, park-keepers and policemen. At the same time he did not object to the principle contained in the resolution ; he thought that was understood. The resolution might be withdrawn that evening and framed in such a manner as to act more justly and equitably to everybody. (Hear, bear.) Councillor ROBERTS sai4 the principle of the resolu- tion had his entire sympathy. A man who had to work throughout the week and was occasionally called upon, in addition, to work on Sunday was entitled to extra pay. He did not think caretakers and policemen would come within the definition of" workmen" in this con- motion.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, July 5, 1.913 (f hind( rijii
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, July 5, 1.913 (f hind( rijii

COMING GARDEN PARTY.—Next Wednesday a garden party, particulars of which are advertised in another column, will be held at the Hamlet, Reddish. The pro- ceeds will go to maintiin a mission child aad other local funds.

COUNTY SCHOLARSITTPS.—In the recent examination for county intermediate scholarships, two girls from the Lymm Grammar School, Ada Joynson and Ruth Willan, were successful in winning scholarships. Ada Joynson distinguished herself by gaining the firth place in the county.
RUSTIBEARING MONDAY.—According to the announce- ment in our advertisement columns, the annual trip to Blackpool from Lymm has been arranged for Rush- heiring Monday.

THE REV. R. W. B. WHITEWAY'S FAREWELL.— There was a large congregation at the Eagle-brow Church on Sunday evening, when the Rev. R. W. B. Whiteway preached his last sermon as supsrintendent minister of the Lymm Primitive Methodist Circuit. Taking as his text Luke xix. 10." For the Son of Alan is come to seek and to save that which was lost," Mr. Whiteway said he was delighted to hear that from all around, people were hungering for the old-fashioned Gospel message which he claimed for his text. Christ's words were feral! men, and his attitude towards the outcast,the poor,the publicans and sinners was a revolu- tion. Later in the evening Mr. Whiteway spoke at an openair service at the Cross.which was under the leader- ship of Mr. J. Waterworth.—On Monday night, Mr. Whiteway delivered addresses at both the senior and junior Christian Endeavour services. During his stay at LyQm Mr. Whiteway has been president of both the localffranch of the British and Foreign Bible Society and the Free Church Council. Mr. and Mrs. Whiteway have received numerous letters and other tokens of the esteem in which the. have been held in the district, and they left for their new circuit at Walkden on Tues- day with the best wishes of a large number of friends.

DOUBLE FATALITY AT EIEATLEY SALT WORKS.— On Wednesday morning a must lamentable accident occurred at Messrs. Charles Moore and Company's Salt Works, Heatlev. It i appears that two men. James Shaw (28), Winwick-road, Warrington, and Thomas Wright (20), Sandy-lane, Lymm, were inside the flues cleaning them out when the boiler-man "blew the steam off." For some reason the steam pipe burst, with the result that the flues were filled with steam. scalding the two unfortunate men in a most terrible manner and rendering them unconscious. They were removei from the flues with all possible speed and a doctor summoned. On his arrival the doctor bad the men conveyed to the Warrington Infirmary. James Shaw, however succumbed to his injuries on Wednes- day afternoon, and Thomas Wright died on Thursday afternoon. The fatality was rendered more tragic by the fact that Staw was a widower with three young children.

div.head: Parish Church Curacy.
div.p: Parish Church Curacy.

The curacy at the Parish Church, which was vacated by the departure of the Rev. A. J. Bratt, will be filled at Christmas by the appointment of Mr. Sydney G. Stanton, who will then be ordained a deacon by the Bishop of the diocese. Mr. Stwton is a graduate of St. John's College, Oxford, and is now a student at Cuddesden Theological College.

div.head: St. James's, Latchford.
div.p: St. James's, Latchford.

The choir festival was celebrated at this church on Sunday, when special music was rendered. At the morning service the preacher was the Rev. W. Brace- camp, vicar of St. Paul's, who said praise was an important factor in public worship, and the function of the choir was to lead. At St. James's, they had a choir that led them reverently, and he appealed to the congregation to support them with their offerings. The Venerable Archdeacon Maitland Wood, vicar of Bowdon, preached at the evening service from the words, " Let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to His name." He spoke of the value of music as an uplifting influence in life, whether it was the music of the wind, of Nature, or of the human voice. The Church laid great stress on the importance of music in the worship of God, and even on a solemn day, such as Good Friday, it was not entirely absent from their services. At the morning service the choir sang the anthem," 0 taste and see" (Goss), and at the evening service" Seek ye the Lord " (Roberts), Mr. E. Davies presiding at the organ.

div.head: Parish Church Old Choristers' Association.
div.p: Parish Church Old Choristers' Association.

The prizes provided by the above association annually for the choir boys of the Parish Church were distributed in Fairfield Schools on Moniay evening. The President (Mr. P. C. Price) presided, and was supported by Messrs. R. T. Harding, F. M. Darby, W. S. Howard, John Green and Walter D-innett. Before calling on the president to distribute the prizes, Mr. Darby, in a few well-chosen remarks, expressed his indebtedness to the association for providing such handsome books, and for the great interest manifested towards the boys. Mr. Price, who had been a member of the choir for upwards of 40 years, then presented the prizes. He said it was a very pleasant duty to reward the good attendance and conduct of the best boys. Ile would be glad if every boy could deserve and receive a prize that night, but those who were left out this time must do their best as model choirboys in the future, and no doubt their turn would come. Every member of a church choir was called upon to help to lead the praises of God in His house. The work should be done with the highest motive and in the very best possible way. He hoped they would all give nothing but their very best. To do that would help theca to grow up to be good and useful men. (Applause.) A very hearty vote of thanks was accorded Mr. Price on the proposition of Mr. R. T. Harding, and seconded by Mr. W. S. Howard. Three rousing cheers were given by the choir boys for the president and committee.

div.head: Church Lads' Brigade.
div.p: Church Lads' Brigade.

At the close of evensong at, the Warring ton Parish Church on Sunday evening, a regimental colour, presented to the 2nd Liverpool Cadet Battalion (Warrington) Church Lads' B:igade, was dedicated by the Rector (Rev. Canon Willis), who is chaplain of the battalion. There was an excellent muster of the boys, under the command of Captain F. M. Aopleton, and the ceremony proved most impressive. The colour takes the form of a silk Union Jack, bearing the arms and motto of the brigade " Figbt the good fight." It has been given to the battalion by Mr. J. Malin Fdelsten, Mr. J. J. Crosfield and Major H. Owen, C.L.B. Immediately after the presentation of the alms, the colour, escorted by Lieutenant F. Bunch (St. Paul's), Colour-Sergeant Gibbs (St. Elphin's), Lance-Corporal Orford (St. Clemento), and Lance-Corporal Astlt7 (Christ Church) was handed to the Rector by Major Brooks. The Rector, laying his hand on the colour, dedicated it in a special form of prayer, after which a general salute was sounded by the buglers of the St. Paul's company. The choir, clergy and escort then formed into procession, and the colour was carried round the church while the hymn "Brightly gleams our banner" was sung. The clergy taking part were the Rector, the Revs. W. Bracecamp (assistant chaplain), T. Vickers and J. M. Ruckinaster. After the Benediction a verse of the National Antbem was sung. Before the boys marched from the church, the Rector addressed them. He said they ought to deem it a great honour to belong to the Brigade, and he exhorted them evert. defend the Church of England, which was the true branch of Christ's Holy Catholic Church in this land.

div.head: Emmanuel Reformed Church, Bold-street.
div.p: Emmanuel Reformed Church, Bold-street.

rhere were good congregations at this church on. Su- nday, when the Sunday school anniversary services were held. The preacher was the Rev. William T. Jaye. Special anniversary hymns were rendered at each service, the singing being led by the childrens choir. In the evening the church choir sang the anthem, "I will sing of Thy mercy," in an expressive manner. A special children's service was held in the afternoon. Praise is due to Mr. J. W. Jovvett (the organist), who was respons- ible for the training of the choir and children.

div.head: " Charles Kingsley : Some Aspects of
div.p: " Charles Kingsley : Some Aspects of
His Life."

At the meAting of the Wycliffe P.S.A. Society on Sunday, Mr. P. M. Oliver gave an address on " Charles Kingsley, and some aspects of his life." He said Kingsley bad a strong insight into the lives of parties around him. He had no patience with shame. The outward surroundings of ideas and reforms were a failure, unless accompanied by the inward and higher ideals of light and truth. Parties, as such, received from him the strongest condemnation of all errors. He felt that a thing to be right must spring from right ideas and motives. The Rev. T. T. James presided, and welcomed Mr. Oliver. Miss Elsie Hewitt sang " Come unto Me" and " Children's home "in a most effective manner. Mr. W. H. Payton presided at the organ. The Wycliffe Baud was in attendance, and accompanied the singing of the hymns, their services being greatly appreciated. Mr. J. W. Travis also took part in the meeting.

St. John's Presbyterian Church. On Sunday the Sabbath school anniversary services were held at St. John's The preacher in the morning was the Rev. William Reid, minister of St. John's, and in the afternoon an address wac delivered by the Rev. J. S. Chedburn. In the evening the church was well filled, and the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. John Mac Neill, Manchester. In a few observations to the children and young people, from the words of Jesus, " Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost," Mr. Mac Neill drew attention to the care that Jesus took of broken things. He cared for the frag- ments. Often they were apt to think God had not time to care for things which were not perfect, and that hearts and lives not perfect might be forgotten or despised by the Heavenly Father, but that was not so. God could repair broken hearts and lives and valued them. The story of the invitations to the king's marriage feast (Matt. xxii. 5) formed the sub- ject of Mr. Mac Neill's general discourse. Solos were very effectively sung by Jean Black and Maggie Mitchell, two young Sabbath school scholars, while a juvenile choir, trained by Miss Dewar, one of the teacners, rendered several children's hymns very creditably. On Monday evening there was a prize distribution, when prizes won in the Presbyterian Church Synodical examinations, etc., were presented to the successful pupils by Mrs. W. Russell, Newholme, Latchford, Mr. Owen officiated as organist at all the services.

div.head: NOVEL ASPARAGUS STEAMER.
div.p: A NOVEL ASPARAGUS STEAMER.

For cooking asparagus the best utensil is a large tin coffee-pot. Its height admits of the asparagus standing on end. Its narrowness prevents the tips from toppling over. The spout gives an outlet in case of the water boiliDg over; and the closed lid allows the tips to steam delicately while the stalks are cooking thoroughly in the deep, rapidly boil- ing water.

COUNCIL AND SUNDAY TRADlNG.—Contiancd. brought about owing to various workmen in the employ of the Corporation having to work shoulder to shoulder, some getting time and a quarter, and others time and a half. If the resolution were adopted it would remove that grievance. The MAYOR said he was advised that the resolution would apply only to those who were paid so much per hour. _ _ _

Councillor WILSON said the resolution would apply to a weekly wage man, but not to an official. Councillor OSBORNE supported the resolution because it was essential that the Corporation should lead the way in regard to conditions of employment. Councillor TAYLOR suggested the appointment of a Wages Board, representing all the committees of the Corporation, to deal with questions of this kind. Councillor DICKENSON : Does the resolution apply to lamplighters? Councillor BRoADHURST : Certainly.

Alderman JAMES EVANS approve a of Councillor Taylor's suggestion and said that if it were carried out they would not find one section of workmen work- ing at a disadvantage compared with other workmen. Asked what he meant by the resolution, Councillor W.H.soN said : I mean all workmen in the employ of the Corporation. I cannot define any parti- cular class. The police will not be affected by it, as they work under special conditions. He added that he had had the assistance of a lawyer in forming the resolution. - - -

Alderman TINNION : That accounts for it. (Laughter.) The MAYOR pointed out that nurses in the employ of the Corporation worked on Sunday. Councillor WILSON: I would include nurses and the whole lot in the resolution. If they work on Sunday they should be paid time and a half. The resolution was carried. The MAYOR: I give notice that at the next meeting of the Council I shall introduce a motion to define the term" workman."

div.head: HATTON.
div.p: HATTON.

MOTHERS' MEETING.—The members of the mothers meeting connected with St. Luke's Mission, Hutton, to the number of about 30, journeyed to Frodsham on Friday of last week. Mrs. Seeker had charge of the arrangement and was ably assisted by Mts. Lee-Jones. and Miss Lee-Jones. The Vicar also journeyed with the party. A brake from the Patten Arms conveyed the party to Overton. En route they called at the residence of Mr. J. E. Seeker, Daresbury, where a walk round the beautiful grounds was much appreciated. Tea was pro- vided by Mrs. Parker-Horse. Mersey View, after which the ladies indulged in various amusements. The party returned home about 8 o'clock.

div.head: WIN WICK.
div.p: WIN WICK.

MARRIAGE or Miss SWEETLOVE.—The marriage was solemnized at St. Oswald's Church, Winwick, of Mr. William Milne Leather, son of Mr. Samuel Leather, High-street, Newton-le-Willows' 3nd Miss Marion Sweetlove, daughter of the late Mr. Wm. Sweetlove and Mrs. Mary Sweetlove. the Post Office, Winwick. The Rector (Rev. Canon Penrhyn) officiated. The bride was given away by her uncle, Mr. Henry Sweetlove. She wore a beautiful dress of white satin and carried a bouquet of lilies. Her ornament was a gold troc.ch, the gift of Mrs. Penrlayn. She was attended by Miss Ethel Yates. who was attired in pale blue viole. Her bouquet was composed of roses and she wore a pendant, the gift of the bridegroom. Mr. Wm. Sweetlove acted as hest man. The happy couple, who were the recipients of many handsome presents, later left for the honey- moon at Stratford-on-Avon.

div.head: PADGATE. WALKING DAY.
div.p: PADGATE. WALKING DAY.

The village was en fete on Saturday, the occasion being the annual Walking Day. The weather condi- tions proved quite satisfactory and the coolness and absence of dust made walking a pleasure. This year the Church of England schools led the procession. Headed by the band of the Cottage Homes, the Vicar, (Rev. G. W. Dickinson), and several officials they first marched to the Farmer's Arms, Fearnbead, and, turning there. proceeded to the other extreme of the village—the junction of Padgate-lane with Orford-road. Again turning here the processiouists retraced their steps until the Wesleyan Church was reached. Here the National anthem was sung by the whole assembly, and the various schools dispersed. In the Church of England section of the procession decorated mail carts were a pleasing feature. Second in the order of progress came the children from the Cottage Homes, whose neat appearance evoked, as usual, much favourable comment. .Then fol- lowed the Wesleyans, who were headed by the Rev. E. Morgan and the officials of the church and school. A touch of colour was given by a number of scholars who represented the characters in an operetta a few weeks ago. The Risley Independent Methodist School brought up the rear, and. though smaller in numbers, were decidedly the favourites from a decora- tive point of view. Among beautiful designs in mail- carts and lurrifs, was a peculiarly appropriate tableau (considering the fact of its being ths local Alexandra Day). This representation was of a sick child in a cot, with a nurse in attendance, and illustrated the Scriptural passage, " Inasmuchlas ye did it unto one of the least of these, ye did it unto Me." In the case of each of the schools, tea was served and afterwards sports were held, and proved highly attractive.

div.head: KING'S LANCASHIRE TOUR.
div.p: KING'S LANCASHIRE TOUR.

Police Communication To Motoristg. Well done, Holland; Well done, Jonathan The Lancashire Automobile Club has received from Well done, John Bull! the Chief Constable of Lancashire, Mr. 11. P. P. Lane, a description of the routes by which the King and Queen will travel on their Lancashire tour, with the approximate timrs of starting and finishing on each day. The letter add; : "Their Majesties' motor-car will carry the Royal Standard, and to prevent confusion it is earnestly desired that motorists of your Union should refrain from carrying any fiagi on their own private cars when travelling in this district during the time of their Majesties' tour. "I should be glad if members of your Union would, as far as possible, avoid using the roads over which their Majesties will travel on these particular dates, and if obliged to use them it would greatly assist the police if they would pay prompt attention to direc- tions given by those on duty as t ) pulling up' to allow their 2,fajesties free and uninterrupted passage. "Further,l would warn you that in county boroughs through which their Majesties will pass the roads will be closed to all vehicular traffic for two hours or more, pending the passage of their Majesties."

[To THE EDITOR OF THE "EXAMINER.") Sir,—l remember at the Free Trade Inter- national Congress held in London, 1908, the Secretary of the Dutch Free Union telling us that the prospects of Free Trade in Holland were gloomy, and there was great danger that the Protectionist party would be successful in changing the fiscal policy of a moderate 5 per cent. duty on manufactured goods for revenue purposes to a higher duty designed for protective ends. Since then, the "Tariff Reform" party have advocated a 12 per cent. all-round duty, and only last week the electors made their pronounce- ment on this proposal. The result has been the overthrow of the Pro- tectionist groups andi government, and a substantial majority elected for the mainten- ance of a low duty for revenue purposes. As in our elections here, there were, no doubt, other issues involved, but it was agreed that "Tariff Reform" was a dominating one. Both Liberals and Socialists have gained at the expense of the Protectionist party. The result is all the more satisfactory because a bait similar to that held out in this country by Mr. Bonar Law and Lord Lansdowne was offered to the voters. The extra revenue derived from the protective taxes was to be earmarked for social reform. The bait has not been swallowed. Well done, Holland! The United States of America are abolishing their food taxes and more than halving their general import taxes. Well done, Jonathan The United Kingdom is keeping the Free Trade flag at the peak and the Protectionate flag is haimast and in tatters. Well done John Bu • CHARLES E. PARKER. , Penketh, June 30, 1913..
