div.head: FOUR 'VISITS IN TWO CENTURIES.
div.p: FOUR 'VISITS IN TWO CENTURIES.

From the day when the carriage of ' George IV. rolled from the George Inn (henceforward so called in his honour) until the visit of Edward VII. in July, 1909, no English Monarch, so far as is known, had driven through the streets of Warrington. Royal visits to Warrington have, indeed, been few and long between—only four are on record during the past two centuries, and to count a fifth we go back another century to the famous visit of Henry VII. in 1495. In earlier centuries when the North road was so largely used, many monarchs follow- ing both warlike and peaceful purposes, must have crossed the old bridge or waded the ford at Warrington. In the absence of reliable records, we are left to form our own conjectures as to these earlier royal passages, and this we propose briefly to do for our readers.

div.head: SAXON RULERS.
div.p: SAXON RULERS.

There is an inscription upon the beam of the Pickering Arms at Thelwall which states that " King Edward the Elder founded a citie here and called it Thelwall." This may or may not be a bit of history. The probabili- ties are in its favour, for the daughter of Alfred the Great resided in Edisbury and held the Cheshire side of the Mersey. It may easily, therefore, have happened that Alfred's son and successor decided to place a small stronghold in Cheshire, and Thelwall may have been the site selected. Though we cannot suggest that the great Alfred ever made his way through the cluster of mud huts that occupied the site of Church- street, it is quite likely that Edward, his. successor, passed among them and crossed the river at the old ford that communicated with Cheshire. KING JOHN.

The elaborate celebrations which Liverpool recently made to commemorate the giving of its charter remind us that King John, of unhappy memory, also visited these parts. It was from the weak and cruel King that Liverpool received its charter in 1207, and at one period of his reign he visited that city as well as Lancaster. He also would cross the Mersey at the old ford at Warrington, though unfortunately no record has been preserved of his visit.

div.head: EDWARD I.
div.p: EDWARD I.

It may be definitely stated, too, that Edward 1., a century later, was a visitor— probably a frequent though casual visitor to Warrington. His Scottish campaign often brought him north, and he took the road that led through Warrington. He was at Preston in 1306, and on this occasion certainly passed through the town. EDWARD 11.

His son also, the vanquished of Bannock- burn, paid a flying and unceremonious visit in 1322. He had sent the Earl of Lancaster to an ignominious death on the charge of being in agreement with the Scots, and was

div.head: LITERARY GLEANINGS.
div.p: LITERARY GLEANINGS.
BENCH AND BAR.

Mr. A. H. agelbach in his book "Anec- dotes of Bench and Bar" tells a good story of a popular solicitor who called upon another brother of the profession and asked his opinion upon a certain point of law. The lawyer to whom the question was addressed drew him- self up and said, " I generally get paid for what I know." The questioner took half-a- crown from his pocket, handed it to the other, and coolly remarked, "Tell me all you know and give me the change."

div.head: KING EDWARD AT THE TOWN HALL IN 1909.
div.p: KING EDWARD AT THE TOWN HALL IN 1909.

The Mayoress (the late Mrs. Forshaw) being prasented. From left to right :--Mrs. A. 11. Crosfield, Lady Greenall, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Mr. (now Lord) Haldane (Secretary for War), the Town Clerk, the Mayoress. Beyond the Royal Motor, the Earl of Derby.
afterwards Bishop of Ely, gave them a further welcome.

The motives which lay behind the visit to Lancashire were probably such as reflected little credit upon the King. Cold-hearted and crafty, Henry VII. had pursued crooked paths and had shed much innocent blood. Among the cruel murders of which he was guilty was that of Sir William Stanley. Tempted by the wealth of his estate he had sent Stanley to the block and seized his wealth. It was probably to soothe his brother that the visit was proposed and carried out. Earl Derby received the Monarch--his brother's murderer—as graciously as possible and entertained him at Lathom House. Returning from thence on August 4th they spent a night in Warrington, but whether as the guest of Sir Thomas Boteler or Sir Richard Delves we cannot tell. On August sth they left for Manchester, being attended to the boundary of the manor by Sir Thomas Boteler and his tenantry, who, with many good wishes for their safety, bade the Royal guests farewell.

after repulsing General Harrison. But he was hastening to his crowning defeat at Worcester. Disastrously defeated by Cromwell, he fled the country, and made France his home until changed conditions made it possible for him to return as King. The Parish Register of burials has presented a record of the skirmish at War- rington in the entry "Aug. B. (buried) Walter Hoape, servant of the Duke of Buckingham." Wounded, perhaps, in the fight or fallen ill by the way, he was laid to rest in the churchyard.

div.head: JAMES T.
div.p: JAMES T.

A full century passed before the people of Warrington had again the pleasure of welcoming a Royal cavalcade. The month of August, 1617, trought James I. on a visit to Bewsey Hall, and the honours were done by Mr. Ireland. The old hall, it may be mentioned, had passed into the possession of Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, whom readers of Scott's" Kenilworth" will vividly remember as the husband of Amy Robsart, and the favourite of Queen Elizabeth, but the Earl did not make it a place of residence. King James had been enjoying the luxury of a Royal progress through Scotland after the fashion set by Queen Elizabeth, and was returning by way of Lancashire. He had a large and imposing retinue, among them the Bishop of Chester, his Chaplain the Earl of Pembroke, and Sir Edmund Trafford, High Sheriff of Lancashire. At Lathom he was worthily entertained by the Earl of Derby, and on August 20th left for Warrington to be received by Sir Thomas Tildesley, Sir Gilbert Ireland, Richard Bold, Esq., and his host of Bewsey Hall. James knighted his entertainer and also Lewis Pemberton. James was evidently in the mood for conferring honours, and knight- hoods were seldom cheaper than when James was making a "Royal progress." At Hoghton Towers on this same journey he conferred the most unusual knighthood that history has any record of. Charmed with the loin of beef he was eating, he raised his sword and exalted it to the dignity of Sir loin. And Sirloin that part of the beast's anatomy has been ever since. On August 21st, 1617, James passed over the bridge to travel to Norton, where he is said to have hunted and killed a buck, his place of entertainment being Rock Savage, the house of Sir Thomas Savage.

div.head: CH ARLES 11.
div.p: CH ARLES 11.
The next "Royal progress" was that ,which Charles 11. made during his attempt to secure the throne. August 16th, 1651, found him pushing his way southward

soon as the Liberals have these aims clearly I defined before them, a new spirit will come over them. It will be as it was with the army of Israelites in the desert when a pillar of fire was appointed to lead them through the night. A clear policy, clearly defined, with the mighty object of making this country a better and nobler living ground for the people—" a treasure ground for the people and not a pleasure ground for the rich "—will rally the party to new effortb and new triumphs.—Harold Spender, in the "Contemporary Review."

div.head: LITERARY UNCLES.
div.p: LITERARY UNCLES.

In our own day we have known uncles of the nursery, men who had but the casual touch of family life. " Alice in Wonderland" was written by a bachelor don of Oxford, and Dodgson always hated any reference to the stories that were written for Alice Liddell. , At Christchurch, Oxford, he was the mathe-

div.head: GEORGE IV.
div.p: GEORGE IV.

Of the visit of the Regent little need be said. No pleasant memories are associated with this vulgar son of Hanover,and we need only say that he slept at the Inn afterwards known as the George, which stood under the shadow of Trinity Church, and was only recently demolished. An unhappy memory lingers over the visit, for when his coach turned the corner to Market Gate, it was discovered that someone had maliciously removed a pin and jeopardised the coach and its occupants. The offence was brought home to an inhabitant who received the punishment of penal servitude, and wore a shackle around his wrist to the day of his death.

div.head: EDWARD VII.
div.p: EDWARD VII.

The most recent Royal visit to Warrington —that of their Majesties King Edward VII. and Queen Alexandra on July 6th, 1909—is still fresh in the memories of the townspeople. Their Majesties called at the town while motoring from a great Territorial review at Worsley to Knowsley Hall. The town was magnificently decorated with triumphal arches, Venetian masts, garlands, flowers and artistic trophies—in fact from end to end of the borough was one long vista of brilliant and varied colour. The Royal car drew up before a green dais at the Town Hall, and the Mayor (Alderman W. J. Forshaw) presented a loyal address of welcome, which had been tastefully illuminated by students of the School of Art. His Majesty handed to the Mayor a reply, in the course of which he said : "Your town and district have witnessed in times past many conflicts between hostile forces, but I am confident that the patriotic spirit of my people is as strong as ever, and that no effort will be wanting to prepare for any risk, however remote." Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., and Lady Greenall, the Borough Member (Mr. A. H. Crosfield) and Mrs. Crosfield were then presented to his Majesty. Miss Edith Forshaw and Miss Bessie Forshaw handed handsome bouquets to Queen Alexandra and Princess Victoria. An additional gift of a diamond necklace was made to Princess Victoria in honour of her birthday, which, by a happy coincidence, was being celebrated on the day of the visit to Warrington. All along the route to Sankey Bridges there were cheering multitudes, and their Majesties were much gratified with the demonstra- tions of loyalty which hailed them on every hand. The rejoicings wound up with a fire- works display in Victoria Park, and a gorgeously illuminated car traversed the tramway routes. A.M.

matical don, and proud only of his mathe- matics. But he will remain as Louis Carroll, with those rooms in "Torn Quod "—and an uncle. Again, one may take the most recent instance of the great child-story that has achieved success—" Peter Pan." That also was written by a man—Sir James Barrie— who, though married, was childless, and had to depend for his inspiration on other people's nurseries. Yet he became the ideal uncle, :Ind the children climb on his knee. On the whole, perhaps, the outsider sees more of the game. Our uncles, when they are Washington Irving, Barrie, Lewis Carroll, are the jolly outsiders who come in and reform the horrible monotony of domestic life. And it must be confessed that the great children's stories have been written by uncles who have never married, never had children of their own, but only taken other people's children on their knee, and talked as to some strange animal with a homing instinct.— Clarence Rook, in " T.P.'s Weekly,"

div.head: now pursuing some of the Earl's followers to Liverpool.
div.p: now pursuing some of the Earl's followers to Liverpool.
lIENRY IV.

The year 1399 witnessed another crossing of the Mersey by one who, though not yet a King, , was on the way to claim the crown. This was Henry of Lancaster. Richard the Second, the weak and wretched King, so vividly portrayed by Shakespeare, broken by his failure in Ireland, had landed in Wales and decided to surrender his throne. Travelling southward, Henry gathered an army as ho went, and crossed the ford with his enthusiastic band, who followed him to Westminster Hall and the Throne.

div.head: HENRY VI.
div.p: HENRY VI.

The middle of the fifteenth century—a period darkened by the Wars of the Roses— again witnessed a Royal visitor. This time it was the unhappy Henry VI. in search of friends and helpers in the counties of Lanca- shire and Cheshire. RICHARD 111.

Richard, Duke of Gloucester, also passed through Warrington when journeying north. Though not yet regarded as a candidate for the throne, it is possible that his plans were laid for attaining it, and everyone knows with what skill, cruelty, and fine courage his plans were carried out. He was travelling on this occasion to Berwick, and there is a tradition that he was the guest of Sir Peter Legh of Bradley Hall.

div.head: HENRY VII.
div.p: HENRY VII.

The first Royal Pageant of which we have any complete record was that of Henry VII. in 1495. This visit was an event of some importance and greatly stirred the town. One very happy result was the erection of a bridge over the Mersey. The Earl of Derby, who was being honoured by the visit, could not allow the King and Queen to be ferried over the river and erected the bridge in their honour. The Royal party arrived at Vale Royal on July 27th, 1495, and slept there as the guests of the Abbot. On July 28th they arrived at Warrington and were the first to pass over the bridge. We may picture in imagination the assemblage which stood by the bridge to welcome him to Lancashire. The Earl of Derby, the donor of the bridge, would be there with his party and wearing the Stanley badge. Sir Thomas Boteler with his tenantry, as representing the more immediate neighbourhood, would probably stand opposite. With him in robes and bands would be the Rector, Sir Richard Delves, and the Hermit Friars headed by Sir Richard Brown would give variety to the scene. _

The King and Queen were surrounded by their own bodyguard of 100 footmen, whose pay was 6d. a day, and they would probably perform the entry upon horseback. The ceremony consisted of the presentation of an address of welcome and the usual greet- ing. Thus received and welcomed into the Duchy of Lancaster by the influential Earl the King and Queen passed through the narrow street S of the town and journeyed to Winwick, where the Rector, Thomas Stanley,

oing. The people cannot wait. Once more the Liberal party has discovered that the law of its being must be always to go for- ward. The result has been most satisfactory. Cabinet committees are now busy with schemes of education, of housing, of land reform. It is stated with some authority that the Board of Agriculture is preparing a scheme under which the State proposes to build 15,000 houses in the country dis- tricts, compulsorily purchasing the land at agricultural value. Mr. Lloyd George, this time urged on by the party instead of being held back, and now at last extricating himself from the poisonous entanglement of Marconi slander, is preparing to take the field. We may prophesy without any termerity that, when once these practical schemes come to birth,all the mimic shadows of Tory reform will disappear. HOW ANIMALS DOCTOR THEMSELVES. When I was a boy I was very fond of cats and used to watch their habits very carefully. One thing I always noticed was that when a cat became ill it always put itself under treatment. It would find out a quiet corner, generally a dark one and lie day and night. The only thing it would take was water; not the most tempting bit of fish would induce it to eat, and it would walk past a saucer of • milk as though it were vinegar. Sometimes [have seen a sick cat go out and eat grass, and.l have seen a dog do the same.
I have since discovered that most animals treat themselves when they are, ill, and instinctively choose food that is best suited to them. •
Let me give you a few points which have been noticed by naturalists.

Many animals, such as stags, elephants, ants, and birds go in for the water cure and bathe themselves. Those suffering from fever restrict their diet, keep quiet,seek darkness and airy places drink much water, and sometimes plung into it from time to time. When a dog ha lost its appetite it eats that species of gras known as "dog-grass." Cats also eat gras catnip, etc., when sick. Sheep and cows i the same circumstances seek out certain herbs. An animal suffering from chronic rheumatism invariably keeps as much as possible in the sun. The warrior ants main- tain regularly organised ambulances. Latreille, the naturalist, cut the antenna of an ant. Other ants covered the wounded part with a transparent fluid from their mouths. If a chimpanzee is wounded it stops the flow of blood by placing its hand on the wound or dressing it with leaves and grass.

A terrier had an injured eye. It remained lying under a counter, avoiding beat and light., although it had been its habit to keep . close to the fire. It adopted a general treat- ment—rest and abstinence from food. The local treatment consisted in licking the upper surface of its paw, which it then applied to the wounded eye, again licking the paw when it became dry. Cats also when hurt treat themselves by this simple method. Delaunay, another naturalist, cites the case of a cat that remained for some time lying on the bank of a river; also that of a cat which had the singular fortitude to remain for forty-eight hours under a jet of cold water. And I suppose everybody has watched the hens as they rid themselves of fleas and other parasites by rubbing their feathers briskly through dust or sand. A JOKE FOR KING GEORGE. One of King George's bobbies in earlier 'years has been to travel about London in a quiet way, and without letting anyone know his rank.

He has been everywhere and seen every- thing. Like his sister, the present Queen of Norway, he greatly liked the old-fashioned horsed 'bus, and knew and patronized every route. He himself has recounted one of his adventures.

Seated immediately behind the driver, he heard the latter say to a troublesome horse, "Come up, yer Royal 'lghness, come up." "Why do you give him that name ? " asked the unknown prince. "Well, y' see, guv'nor," answered John, "that 'oss is so 'aughty and lazy and good for nothing that I—well, I just calls 'im 'ls Royal 'lghness—there ain't nothin' else for
The King chuckled, but did not follow the subject further.
MORE BEECHER STORIES.

The following little stories formed part of my qrticle on Henry Ward Beecher, but were held over through want of space. The first refers to his school days. A class in natural philosophy, not very well prepared, was stumbling through the theory of the tides. "I can explain that," said Henry. "Well, you see, the sun catches hold of the moon and pulls her, and she catches hold of the sea and pulls that, and this makes the spring tides." "But what makes the neap tides?" "Oh, that's when the sun stops to spit on his hands," was the brisk reply. After about six months at this school, Henry was returned to his parents' hands with the reputation of being an inveterate joker and an indifferent scholar.

div.head: PORTRAIT DISCOURAGED HIM.
div.p: THE PORTRAIT DISCOURAGED HIM.

Henry Ward Beecher once turned a good joke upon his sister, Mrs. Harriet Beecher Stowe. Mrs. Stowe, as everybody knows, wrote "Uncle Tom's Cabin." At a dinner party on one occasion, Mr. Beecher began to tell his sister bow the book had been trans- lated into Italian by a monk, and how the monk had sent a letter to him full of adula- tion, and which said that if he could kiss the woman who wrote the book he would die happy. Mr. Beecher added with a twinkle in his eye, "I sent him your portrait, Harriet, and . —well, nothing has been heard of him since."

div.head: THREE TIMES!
div.p: THREE TIMES!

In his undergraduate days Professor Ramsay was a notable athlete, and on one occasion, when distributing prizes in the gymnasium of the Glasgow University, took occasion to pas some scathing remarks on the softness of the .present generation. He illuminated his criticisms from Roman history. " Gentlemen," cried the professor of humanity, " you should do as the ancient Romans. The youths of Rome used to gather on the banks of the Tiber every morning and swim three times across the river."
_ . Voice from his audience: " What did they do about their clothes ? "

When I have time, the friend I love so well Shall know no more those weary, toiling days ; I'll lead her fret in pleasant paths always, And cheer her heart with words of s Neetest praiso When I have time.

When you have time ! The fi iend you hold so dear May be beyond the reach of your intent— May never know that you so kindly meant To fill her dreary life with sweet content When you. had time. Now is the time ! Ab, friend, no longer wait To scatter loving smiles and words of cheer To these around whose lives are now so drear ; They may not need you in the coming year; Now is the time!

div.head: *LIFE AND DEATH.
div.p: *LIFE AND DEATH.
The Secrets that lie Beyond the Grave.
SOME SAVAGE SIDELIGHTS.

"If a man die, shall he live again ? " How many myriads of human beings, oppressed by the mortality of living things and the transient good and happiness of this world, have asked themselves that question ! Ago after age men have agitated themselves with the enigmas of life and death, and have sought to explain the inexplicable. Death is no less a mystery to us than it was to our rude forefathers. We know not a whit more than they what lies "beyond the veil." But although we cannot solve the mystery, it fascinates us. Death is ever present in our midst; we cannot escape it. Against our will we are compelled from time to time to consider the problem of immortality, for death is the most certain fact of our existence. We know that sooner or later each one of us has to make the great adventure. It is not surprising, therefore, that men are pre-occupied with this question of life after death, or that they are ever ready to consider anew the timeworn arguments which are adduced in support of the belief in a life beyond the grave. Our Ultimate Destiny. - -

But it is not the philosophical aspect of the question with which this book is concerned. It is not a meta- physical justification of the belief in immortality that Dr. Frazer offers to his readers. Ho expressly dis- claims such intention. He treats the subject solely from the historical standpoint, and surely an account, however slight, of the diverse beliefs that men have held as to the ultimate destiny of the human spirit cannot fail to be interesting and instructive. For these beliefs have had a profound effect on man's life. Dr. Frazer would not suggest, I think, that a study of the beliefs of savage peoples as to the soul's fate at death is a support to one's own belief. Rather the reverse, if anything. For it shows the crude beginnings from which have arisen the great ieligions of the world.

The difficulties in the way of the historian of religion, however, are no light ones. To trace the rise and growth of religious beliefs requires that we should know the ideas entertained by prehistoric man in regard to himself and his position in the world. It is not enough that we analyse the religious views of the civilised world at the 'present day, since, in great measure, these views are traditional. But how are we to investigate the ideas of peoples who could not write, and who could leave no permanent records of their beliefs? Not directly, certainly, for we have no evidence to go upon. It would appear almost to be a hopeless task. But Dr. Frazer suggests a way by hich we may approximately get at the beliefs of primitive man. It is a commonplace of science that humanity began its upward career at a very low level of culture, a level much below tbat of the lowest existing savages, and that the various races of men have gradually progressed upward, at different rates, until they have reached their present stages of develop- ment. Therefore, it is to the existing savages of to-day that we must betake ourselves and study their notions of life and death and man's fate in the here- after, if we are to get at the ultimate source, the historical origin, of the evolution of religious beliefs.

Savages and Death. Now the first thing that strikes the investigator in this field is the fact that to savage peoples—and all savages would appear to agree in this is not a natural cccurrence at all. "They disbelieve," says Dr. Frazer," in what we call a natural death ; they think that all men are naturally immortal in this life, and that every death which takcs place is in fact a violent death inflicted by the hand of a human enemy, though in many cases the foe is invisible and works his fell purpose not by a sword or a spear but by magic" When a death occurs the relatives and friends at once proceed, though in many cases without success, to ascertain who is respons- ible for it, believing, as they do, that it is attributable to some person or persons who bore to the deceased. Thus among the Indiana of Guiana, "a person dies and it is supposed that an enemy has secured the agency of an evil spirit to compass his death. Some sorcerer, employed by the friends of the deceased f,r that purpose, pretends by his incanta- tions to discover the guilty individual or family, or at any rate, to indicate the quarter where they dwell. A near relative of the dead man is then charged with the work of vengeance. ll° becomes a kanaima, or is supposed to be possessed by the destroying spirit so called, and has to live apat t according to strict rule, and submit to many privations, until the deed of blood be accomplished. If the supposed offender cannot be slain, some innocent member of his family—man, woman or little child—must suffer instead."

There is a distinction observed among some savages letween deaths which are attributed to the indirect action of sorcerers and those attributed to the direct action of dem )ns. The p ractical ccnsequences of this distinction are wry important. Where death is due to sorcery it must, in the opinion of savages, be avenged by killing the suppcsed sorcerer. But death by the action cf a demon cannot be so avenged, for the demon is beycnd the reach of human vengeance. And this distinction involves the deciding on the cccasion of every death whether it occurred through the agency of a demon or a sorcerer. Various methods are employed in order to arrive at this decision, one of the most deadly being the poison ordeal. Thus we learn that a small tribe named Uwet, in the hill- country of Calabar, almost swept itself off the face of the earth by the constant use of this method. On one occasion the whole population drank the poison to prove themselves pure; about half of them perished. Some savages appear, however, to admit certain exceptions, such as extreme old-age, accidents and violence as causes of death which are independent of sorcery; and this admission certainly marks a stage of intellectual progress. Belief in Immortality. • • -•

But believing, as they do, that man was originally immortal in this life, these savages have to account for the fact of death, and accordingly we have a long Belies of myths which profess to explain the origin of death. Dr. Frazer has classified them, and profoundly interesting they are. Dr. Frazer commences his survey of the beliefs and practices that have arisen' in regard to the dead in Australia, the aborigines of Central Australia being the lowest savages about whom we possess accurate information. With one exception, these different tribes in Central Australia believe in a kind of reincarnation. They have no conception of a special world of departed spirits, the souls of the dead being suppcssd to haunt their native land waiting to be reborn into this world as infants. After considering all the races in Austialia we Fuss to the Torres Straits Islands, and thence to the many tribes which inhabit the district of New Guinea and Melanesia. The beliefs and customs of these peoples are all reviewed in great detail, and althcugh exhibiting differences they bear a general resemblance to one another. There is this striking similarity in the beliefs and practices of all these peoples regarding the dead, that while it is possible to interpret some of them as evidences of affection towards the departed, there is far stronger reason for believing that the motive underlying these customs is fear of the ghosts of the dead. It is difficult, if not impossible, to resist the conviction that fear is the dominant characteristic of the beliefs and ceremonies that obtain amongst all savage peoples. Even among the lowest in the scale of civilisation, where superstition is rampant, there are cases of detected imposture, and Dr. Frazer tells an interesting story of a girl in New Guinea who attempted to impose on the relatives of a dead boy by representing herself as a medium capable of effecting communica- tion between the living and the dead. She was dis- covered in the act of personating the spirit of the deceased boy and was sentenced to a short term of imprisonment.

Dr. Frazer declines to draw any inferences as to the truth or falsehood of the belief in immortality from the facts uhich he presents to his readeis. His business, as he conceives it, is not to pass judgment on the forms and customs to which this belief has given rise, but to desciibe them. This Dr. Frazer has done. The book is a perfect storehouse of facts, and will be of immense value to all interested in the stuey of Man. It i 3 a fascinating account of the hopes and fears, the deepest thoughts and the highest flights of the imagination of those who live on the outskirts of civilisation.
A. W. PERRIS. *" The Belief in Immortality, and the Worship of the Dead." By J. G. Frazer, D.C.L , etc. Vol. 1. 10s. Macmillan and Co. Ltd.

div.head: WAGES AND FOOD.
div.p: WAGES AND FOOD.
Town Council Debate on Local Health Conditions.
FIGHTING CONSUMPTION.

The health conditions of Warrington were under discussion at a special meeting of the Town Council, held an hour before the ordinary monthly meeting on Tuesday evening, for the purpose of discussing the annual report of Dr. J. Coote Hibbert, who until recently was Medical Officer of Health for the borough. The attendance was far from suggesting a great interest in questions of such vital importance to the community, for at the appointed time five o'clock it was not possible to form a quorum, and until the usual monthly business was reached, there was a very poor muster. The Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph) presided. The discussion ranged over a variety of topics, including housing, wages, and the smoke nuisance.

div.head: SAVING CHILD-LIFE.
div.p: SAVING CHILD-LIFE.

Alderman JAMES EVANS, as chairman of the Health Committee, opened the debate by expressing the regret that, considering the importance of the business, tbe attendance was so sparse. Continuing, he said the annual report of the Medical Officer of Health showed figures which must go to prove that considerable improvement had been made, especially with regard to child-life, within the borough. The infantile mortality rate for the year under report was 92 per 1,000, the lowest on record. The general death-rate was just half the rate it was 50 years ago, viz :—ln 1861 it was 28 per I,ooo,and in 1912, 14 5 per 1,000. The new area in municipal government commenced with the passing of the Public Health Act, 1875. The years 1876 to 1879, during which period Dr. Joseph, the present Mayor, occupied the position of Medical Officer of Health, saw the starting of those measures of sanitation which the Public Act made necessary, and which had formed the ground work of public health administration in Warrington. (Applause.) The first important step taken was the building of the first portion of our Fever Hospital, which was opened for the reception of patients in 1877. Eight thousand nine hundred and nineteen patients had passed through Aitkin-street Hospital, and the death-rate for cases treated in the hospital was only 7 per cent, which was an exceptionally low rate, when they remembered that in addition to scarlet fever they treated diphtheria and enteric fever—two very acute diseases.

div.head: CLOSING INSANITARY HOUSES.
div.p: CLOSING INSANITARY HOUSES.

Under the Housing of the Working Classes Act of 1890, and the Housing and Town Planning Act of 1909, considerable work had been done to remove or improve the undesirable, dark, damp, or badly-ventilated dwell- ings. During the last 22 years, that was since the Housing Acts came into operation, the Health Com- mittee had closed 251 houses, and had had improve- ments made in 280 other houses. That, of course, was in addition to repairs to property carried out under the Public Health Act, 1875. The Health Committee were indebted to the Paving and Sewerage Committee for the paving of the streets and passages, but more considerably to the Water Com- mittee for providing them with a pure and sufficient water supply such as they had at the present time. In 1810, the only supply of water for domestic purport( was from wells sunk in close proximity to the dwell- ings. In 1846, the Warriagton Waterworks Company was constituted, and in 1847 they had the Appleton Reservoir constructed. The water from Appleton was used for domestic purposes until:about 1870, when the Winwick wells were first brought into use with their excellent quality of water. (Hear, hear.) THE FIGHT AGAINST CONSUMPTION.

The disease most prominently before their notice at the present time was tuberculosis, but, as the Council would see from the annual leport, the Health Com- mittee were taking steps to deal with cases of that disease. He wished to assure the town that there was no slackness or lack of effort en the part of the local authorities with regard to sanatorium treatment. They had at present 17 cases under treatment in Sankey Sanatoriumoand when the Local Government Board had sanctioned the scheme they would be prepared to treat 10 patients. The responsibility for the delay in carry- ing out the scheme did not rest with the Health Com- mittee, but with the Local Government Board, who had objected to it on the ground of expense—an unusual experience. Revised plans had been in the hands of the Board for five weeks, but nothing had been heard of them. Since the Sanatorium was opened in August, 1911, for the treatment of phthisis cases, they had had 66 admissions, both insured and non- insured persons, and the Health Committee felt that it was impossible to calculate the good that this hospital bad done, not only to the patients themselves, but to the general public. "LIFE AND DEATH."

In conclusion, the Alderman pointed out that the Health Committee was not a profit-aarning department in the ordinary sense, but it was concerned with issues of life and deatb. Ile hoped, therefore, that in con- sidering the proposals which they brought forward from time to limo the Council would allow them consider- able latitude, and they would not be afraid to give a good account of their stewardship. (Applause)

div.head: MORE IMPORTANT THAN PROFITS.
div.p: MORE IMPORTANT THAN PROFITS.

Alderman BRNNF.rr, having referred to the dis- couragement which the extremely small attendance engendered, alluded to Alderman Evans's remark that the Health Committee was not a prat-earning com- mittee. He (the speaker) was never able to understand why they should calculate everything by spending and earning in hard cash. Earning was not the most import- ant thing in life. The health and real welfare of the community was influit2ly more important than any purely cash transaction, and a good many of their municipal mistakes arose from the fact that they did not judge things by their real value. (Hear, hear.) If they could minimize suffering or disease and give a longer and a pleasanter life they would be doing the best thing it was possible for a Corporation to do, and money expended in that direction was not badly expended. (Hear, hear.) THE CANCER SCOURGE.

It was satisfactory to find that the infantile death- rate was the lowest on record. If they could save infant lives and give the children a chance of develop- ing into good and useful citizens they could not over- estimate the ultimate consequences. Reference was made in the report to a horrible disease—cancer. Its prevalence in these days was alarming. It was a disease with which the medical profession did not seem to be able to grapple successfully. There were 59 deaths from the disease during the year in Warrington. Experimental work probably did not come within the scope of the committee, but, in view of all that had been claimed for radium, it would be worth while try- ing it in Warrington as a means of mitigating the cancer scourge.

div.head: HOUSING AND DEATH-RATES.
div.p: HOUSING AND DEATH-RATES.

The Alderman next called attention to the fact that the death-rates almost automatically followed the characteristics of the various wards. In districts which were densely populated, with houses built at the rate of forty or fifty to the acre, and with no open sploas, the death-rate was high. If the houses were St for decent people to live in, with gardens and the opportunities of enjoying fresh air and recreation, the death-rate was low. Ihmley Ward, for instance, had a death-rate of 192, Bewsey 182, St. John's 17 3, and St. Austin's (one of the most desirable wards in the town) 10-7. Therefore, he contended, the Corporation were responsible for the state of things which existed. With regard to the housing problem, he would prefer to see it solved by private enterprise, but they had to take social conditions as they found them, and as long as wages were so irregular and so low, they would never get really satisfactory housing conditions, except by State or municipal schemes. HOUSES AND SEWERS.

Councillor GOUGH contended that the Health Com- mittee had acted inconsistently in closing some houses, while they allowed air shafts to be put in others. The improvement in the water supply had justified the expenditure, but another matter of vital importance, which still remained to be dealt with, was the sewering of the town. The stench which emanated from some of the sewers was dangerous to health. " IIIE BRISTLING FORCES OF VESTED INTERESTS."

Councillor HENSHALL said that no more important report had ever been submitted to the Council than that of their former Medical 011izer. Considering the difficult, delicate and complex matters with which the Health Committee had to deal, and the bristling forces of the vested interests that surrounded them, he was lost In admiration for the manner in which they did their work. (Hear, hear.) From the report he saw with reference to the work at the Sankey Sanatorium that in ten cases the disease of consumption "had apparently been arrested." It needed no imagination to picture the opportunity that bad come into those ten lives through the work of the Health Committee— the introduction of the element of hope so vital to the enjoyment of life and the accomplishment of any real work. But many patients had also greatly improved. The committee was not a profit-earning committee in the ordinary sense, but in the deepest and highest sense it was, for it was impossible to set an economic value on the lives ahich were being saved through its efforts. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: WAGES AND FOOD.
div.p: WAGES AND FOOD.

Councillor PEMBERTON did not agree with Alderman Bennett's inferences as to the causes of the rates of mortality in the various wards. It was not altogether the number of houses to the acre that caused a high death rate. Where they bad a great number of people with continuous low wages the vitility could not be the same in the matter of resisting disease, because the people had not the necessary food to build up the frame as it ought to be built up. Children from their infancy did not get it, as their parents had to bay in the cheapest shops. If the children in Bold-street had to (Continued in Next Column.)

div.head: LAND POLICY OF THE LABOUR PARTY.
div.p: THE LAND POLICY OF THE LABOUR PARTY.

Sir,—The report of the committee of the Labour Party has been published, and it is an interesting document for all concerned with land reform. In spite of the presence on the committee of Messrs. Barnes and Parker the report is disappointing to land reformers. For they recognise nowhere in this report that the land question is the bottom question. They set out three objects to aim at :- 1. .To appropriate land values to social uses. 2. To secure the highest possible productivity of the land.
3. To or sure good wages and a full life to all rural workers.
These are excellent objects, but the actual reforms they suggest do not even pretend to secure any of them, or even to be a step in their dirsztion. The actual measures they recommend are

a. The extension of the Wages Board Act•.to agricultural labourers. The Board, and the impartial arbitrators that we know so well, are to determine a minimum wage in each district, guided, of course, by the lowest on which the labourer can live and breed, and the highest that the " industly can bear." To those who have had the experience of the minimum wage for coal miners, one need hardly point out the dangf,r that this may remit in the less competent losing their jobs, and the consumers ming a higher price. Wages can only go up without prices going up too, when labour has more opportunities of employ- ing itself in producing more goods. Oppoitunity, not a Board and officials, i 3 what is wanted. b. State aid fir rural housing. The State is to build cottages for the labourer and let them to him .at what are known as charity rents. For this also a Bill has been already introduced by the Conservative 'Party. The landlords have still to find housing for the four-legged stock on the farms, but it would doubtless be very pleasing to them that the State should take over from them the housing of the other sort of stock. The cheaper you can house labour, the less you need to pay labour. In old days the farmers used to be assisted by the parish helping the labourer v; ith out- door relief. That also proved a valuable means of keeping down the wages bill. One might add that it iv uld be only the bad landlords who would be helped by this fancy scheme; the good ones find houses for their labourers already. c. Fair rent courts for the farmer. Again, the inevitable Board is to determine the rents to be paid by the farmer. It is common knowledge that rents are now being raised when a change of tenancy occurs; or in other words thnt farms are now let to sitting tenants at rents below those which could be got. Is the Board going to raise these rents, an unpopular course? Or is it g ing to keep them as they are, and so convert the tenant into so much of a landlord? In any case where do the public come in? We should be stereotyting the existing large farms, and placing a formidable barrier in the way of more intensil e cultivation.

d. Credit banks with State support. This it also very popular with landlords and the Conservative party. Of course, under existing circumstances, the easier you make it for farmers to borrow capital, the more demand there will be for the landlords' land,and the higher rents they will be able to get. Why not credit banks for shopkeepers or insurance agents? Why sbould farmers be the only class helped? The answer is simple; such kind assistance increases the value of agricultural land. e. Amendment of the Small Holdings Acts, so as to enable County Councils to buy at Budget valuation prices, especially land near towns. Why should the country be burdened with purchasing land at the present inflated prices? Compel the people who own this sort of land to pay their rates on their land on its selling value, and the prices will soon be more reason- able. It will then hardly need a Council and its °facials to come between the man who wants land and the land be wants.

Take these practical proposals one by one, and inquire diligently how they even pretend to secure the three objects at which the Labour party say they aim. Do any of them—a, b, c, d, or e —take land values for sccial uses? Do they secure the highest possible oductivity ? Which of them even tends in that direction? The Minimum Wage would induce a farmer to employ fewer hands, not more. The fixing of rents would check even the present movement towards small holdings and intensive cultivation. Do they ensure good wages? Which, besides the first, pretends to do so? and those who have most experience of a legal minimum wage know that, too, is a broken reed.

The Labour Party's objects are excellent, but their methods have no visible connection with their objects. If they were really to go straight for their objects they would have to attack landlordism to attack the land monopoly, Is it that they are afraid? Why do they not point out that production, and therefore employment, is at present restricted, because all agricultural improvements are burdened with rates and tales? That production and useful work is restricted because large areas of land are held out of use, or put to an inferior use, owing to an absurd system of rating which is based on the use of land, and not on the value of the land whether used or not ? They do not hint at any, even the slightest, reform of the rating system, or at the taxation of land values. These, by forcing land into use and conse- quently reducing its price, by relieving all the pro- ducts of industry from taxation, would do more to increase wages and secure a larger production of wealth than all the palliatives they could suggest in a welvemonth.

Wages do not come down from heaven, or even from some beneficent Board or Government depart- ment. They Come from the land and are produced by labour working on the land. Any real reform will have to bring land and labour nearer together, it will have to increase the supply of land that men can use. This is the bottom of the wages question, and all else, housing, credit, and above all independence depends on the wages question. Our Labour Party migbt well take a leaf out of the book of the Labour parties in South Africa, or in New Zealand, or even in the despised Argentine. Each of these place the taxation of land values at the front of their programme as the means of tackling the land question. Read the manifesto of the South African Labour Party, when they are dealing with the wages question : " In the Transvaal there are large tracts of mining land lying idle and waiting for the owner to reduce his price before it can be worked. There are vast areas of fertile farming land held out of use by specu- lating land companies. In the towns great numbers of valuable building sites are kept vacant or only partially used because the owners are waiting for a rise. Miners cannot work on mining land that the owner keeps idle. Farmers cannot farm without farming land. Builders cannot build without land to build on.

"Tax the value of mining land and the owners will have to work it; more jobs for miners. Tax the I value of farming land and the farmers will be able to get land easily; more farms for farmers. Tax the value of building land—the owners must use it or sell to someone who will use it—more opening for builders and allied trades. "When the miners and farmers and builders are busy then the commercial and trading community are also busy, and, in fact, everybody benefits. Wages will be good and unernp:oyment minimised, thus helping the worker to recover his independence." It is a pity that we cannot import the South African Labour Party.
- JOSIAH L, WEDGWOOD. House of Commous, S.W.

which he has had a most successful term of service. As a preacher (writes a correspondent), he carefully prepares for his pulpit, and his sermons always are educative and inspiring and lighted up by an earnest- ness that never fails to draw men to the higher ideals of Christian character and life. div.head: Rev. W. Cooper's Farewell.
div.p: Rev. W. Cooper's Farewell.

The Rev. W. eloper concluded his ministry at the Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church on Sunday. Althmigh no special adverti,ing had taken place and it had further been announced that no farewell sermon would be preached, a splendid c mgregation assembled at all the services. During the announcements in the evening, Mr. Cooper took occasion to speak of his connection with the church, Sunday school, Christian Endeavour and the choir, which had always been of a very satisfactory character. On all occasions his people and officers bad most heartily co-operated with him in all the efforts engaging their attention. He had only been there for three years, but they had been the happiest three years, in his life. He had received nothing but kindness from the people, and he severed his connection with the Primi- tive Methodist circuit with• keen regret. It was not his fault that he was going away, nor yet the fault of his people, but because of a definite inner call to another sphere of work. Whilst his clnnections with his own circuit had been most satisfactory, he had nothing but good to say about his relationships with the affairs and the people of the town. His views had not always coincided vith those of his contempofaries, but he had always been accorded the fairest of treat- ment and consideration. He had received many expressions of regard and esteem which were excep- tionally encouraging. Mrs. Wright, their mutual friend, had sent a communication, as had also his Worship the Mayor. Mr. Cooper urged his members to extend to his successor, the Rev. A. J. Chessum, as warm a welcome as they had accorded him and his wife, and that if they would continue to co-operate with their minister, as they had done in the past, their future success was assured. - - .

Preaching from the text" The secret of the Lord is with them that fear Inn," Mr. Cooper said that whilst fear had been the dominant note of ancient religion this was now supplanted by love. In the Christian dispensation, the secret of the Lord was interpreted as conversion—a personla acceptance of the finished work of Christ. _

Several favourite hymns were sung, and the choir, under the able conductorship of Mr. A. Spruce, sang Woodward's anthem The radiant morn bath passed away." Mr. Banner officiated at the organ. Mr. Cooper commences his new ministry in the Leigh circuit to-morrow (Sunday), when he will preach at Glazebury. The circuit comprises two churches in Leigh, and one each at Platt Bridge, Abram, Glaze- bury, Glazebrook and Cadishead. Mr. Chessum will commence his ministry at Legh- street on July 20th.

div.head: SUGAR WORKS FIRE. £5,000 DAMAGE AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: SUGAR WORKS FIRE. £5,000 DAMAGE AT EARLESTOWN.

During the early hours of Sunday morning one of the night workmen at the works of the Sankey Sugar Company, sugar refiners, Earlestown, discovered an outbreak of fire in one of the warehouses contain- ing a large quantity of refined sugar. As there was grave danger of the flames spreading to several other buildings, the sugar was removed from the warehouses as far as possible. Three fire brigades appeared on the scene, and just about six o'clock the flames were got under control. One warehouse was completed gutted, and a large quantity of sugar rendered useless. The origin of the fire is at present unknown. The damage, which is estimated at about £5,400, is believed to be covered by insurance.

Then, again, people did not live in hovels from choice, but because they had not the means to pay higher rents. Ile did not believe in municipal hotising schemes, but contended that the payment of a decent wage to every worker would do more to solve the difficulty. By building houses, Corporations would be helping to keep wages down. If they went in for housing the people, surely they would not deny them bread, which was more essential.

div.head: IMPROVED WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: IMPROVED WATER SUPPLY.

The MAYOR, in commenting upon satisfactory features of the report, said three great evils had been removed since 1874, mainly owing to the work of the Health Committee. There was first of all, the use of Appleton water as a drinking water, which was at one time a prolific source of typhoid fever; he attended 100 cases himself during a few winter months. Another step forward, was the abolition of the use of pump water, and of the back-to-back house system. The improved condition of the water and the improved ventilation had certainly done a great deal to lower the death rate of Warrington—a fact of which they were all proud. Credit was also due to them for the decrease in the infantile mortality rate, and the deaths from measles and diphtheria, which were much below the rates of other great towns, or even the United Kingdom. Aldermsn EVANS, in reply, pointed out that the ques- tion of the sewers came under the control of the Paving and Sewerage Committee. With reference to the intro- duction of shafts, to which Councillor Gough had alluded, they had to consider the surroundings of certain small houses, and the shafts had been allowed in twenty hr.uses. Alderman TINNION pointed out that it was an exceed- ingly difficult matter to ventilate sewers, and what might be effective in one case would not be in another. The debate closed without apy proposition being brought forward.

div.head: COUNCIL AND THE SMOKE ABATEMENT BIL
div.p: COUNCIL AND THE SMOKE ABATEMENT BIL
PROFESSOR GRAHAM AND THE MAYOR.
[TO THE EDITOR or THE "EXAMINER."]

Sir,—The Mayor of Warrington criticises in your issue of Juno 14th the Smoke Abatement Bill which has been read a first time in the House of Commons, after elaborate consultation with local authorities all over the country for a period of three years. His main point is that local authorities should not be interfered with by the Local Government Board or any central authority, but should be allowed to go on neglecting their duty in regard to smoke as so many of them do now. From a place with Warrington's dirty atmosphere particularly, it is somewhat amusing for the Mayor to speak about a properly constituted local authority being worthy of being trusted with the conduct of its own affairs. Everyone knows that in the matter of Smoke Abatement the Warrington authority is one of the most conspicuous failures in the whole country. Other municipalities are, however, better minded if less-confident, and I am glad to say that the memorial on which the Bill was based, and which con- tained its principal provisions, has the definite suppprt of twenty-nine of the largest municipalities in the country, including Manchester, Liverpool, Bradford, Glasgow, Belfast, and others. I may also inform him that we have all along been aware that the relations between the Central Government and the local authorities constituted a question of the utmost delicacy, and we think it is something of a triumph to have been able to carry with us the representatives of nearly all the most important municipilities in the country. The Bill is carefully drafted, so that no authority which does its duty will be interfered with. Objection arises from local authorities which do not want to do their duty. The temper in which Dr. Joseph meets this attempt at benefiting his town is best shown by the fact that he complains that while we do too much, beyond what science at present enables us to d?, with regard to factories, we do too little with regard to dwelling-houses. The fact is that we have carefully considered how far we could go with both these sources of pollution, and are perfectly satisfied that the experience of an increasing number of manufacturers shows that the possibilities which science has placed at our disposal are far from being realised ; but further that it is not yet possible to make legislation to the effect that every house has to use only gas or electric stoves and cookers, which are at present the only universal means of getting rid of domestic smoke.

With regard to the relative quantity of dome3tic and manufacturing smoke, which after all is a bye- issue, opinion ia Manchester has settled down to the belief that in this great centre of population domestic smoke is responsible for about one half of the total ; but in a place of transgressors like Warrington heel sure that it is responsible for a comparatively insignificant amount. The Mayor criticises the fact that the Local Govern- ment Board exemptions, which with great moderation we propose, only last ten years. He seems to forget what we considered, that at the end of that time the power can be renewed if necessary. The Mayor's statement that whatever legislation applies to works should apply to houses, shows how little he has studied the question. Eveiyone knows that it is much easier to deal with a fire in the firebox of a boiler than in the firegrate of a kitchen. At the end of his interview I notice with astonish- ment that the Mayor credits himself with "practical comtron sense," and in the same breath says that smoke is not as injurious to health as it has been represented. Let him consider the mortality tables of Dr. Niven, which show the sudden and large increase in the deaths from lung dis 'use inevitably following each outbreak of those fogs into which sm, ke enters in concentrated form.
Warrington would do well to take the advice of Aldei man 13ent ett. _
JOHN W. GRAIUM (Chairman of the Smoke Abatement League). Dalton Hall, Victoria Park, Manchester.

div.head: "FEEBLE AND SPASMODIC
div.p: "FEEBLE AND SPASMODIC
EFFORTS."
Town Council Have Done "A Little " To Control Smoke,
[To TIIE EDITOR or THE " EXAMIXER."]

Sir,— I am delighted to see that the" Examiner "' is continuing its protest against those conditions which prevent Warrington becoming a residential town in which the inhabitante can enjoy sunshine, pure air, and cleanliness. There is happily a growing desire for better conditions of home life and especially a growing appreciation of the value of fresh air and sunshine. The smoke, while far from the only handicap which those who reside in Warrington have to bear, is a very serious one and it is largely unnecessary. The Town Council and Health Committee in their feeble, perfunctory, and spasmodic t fforts to control the smoke nuisance have effected a little, but it is only a little. They have handicapped their inspectors by the adoption of an exceptionally absurd time limit for the emission of black smoke, and have altogether neglected the powers (limited though they be) over those trades connected with the smelting of ore, calcining, puddling, and rolling of metals,and the con- version of pig iron into wrought. Whether this last is due to ignorance of their power to control these trades, or, as it has been more than once suggested, to fear, it is difficult to say. In comparatively small towns like Warrington it is almost impossible to get together a Health Committee formed of individuals strong enough to perform the statutory obligations, and to be independent enough to act with fear- lessness in protecting the general com- munity against the carelessness of large and influential manufacturers. In such a town you are sure to have a considerable number on the Council and Health Committee who, in some way or other, for personal reasons, are not disposed to take a course, even in the public interest, which may be in any way troublesome to these big local interests. The pro- posed new Act wisely provides, if the Local Govern- ment Board think it desirable, for the constitution of authorities covering larger areas where personal considerations are not so likely to interfere with the public trust. It is unfortunate that this is necessary. If the powers already in existence were exercised ittith fearlessness there would be little need of an amend- ing Act. A certain amount of smoke we must have ; no one can, in view of our present knowledge and difficulties, expect a manufacturing town to be free from it. Of course, it is a favourite custom of those who would do nothing to represent those who contend for abatement as utopian and unreasonable individuals. Such is not the case. It is becaus3 we know that a great deal of the smcke, which, like a trailing black flag, so often adorns the Warrington chimneys, is largely due to carelessness, badly constructed furnaces and over- worked boilers. Those who live in the town have a just right to protest against the continuance of these preventable conditions, and to expect that the authorities will, without fear or favour, exercise dip powers and fulfil the duties entrusted to them. Let the "Examiner "keep up its protest.
ANTI-SMOKE.

div.head: COUNCIL DISCUSSION.
div.p: COUNCIL DISCUSSION.

The smoke nuisance gave rise to some at the meeting of the Warrington Town C Tuesday evening, and it transpired that 1,1 Committee had refused to support the Stool rnent Bill on the ground that it would unduly with local industries. In the course of the the annual report of the Medical Officer of E

ALDERMAN BENNETT'S DISSATISFAI Alderman BENNETT said the Health Comm doing a little better, in dealing with the nub he was far from satisfied. Warrington F.C.'s Fixtures for Next
Season. CAPITAL HOLIDAY PROGRAMME.

Below we publish Warrington Football Club's League fixtures for the season 1913-14. The fresh attractions are :—Hull Kingston Rovers, Dewsbury and Batley. The fixture witty Wakefield Trinity has not been renewed. A capital list of holiday fixtures has been arranged by the new secretary (Mr. T. B. Bradshaw). Oldham will be the visitors on Boxing day, Dewsbury on Good Friday, and Hull Kingston Rovers on Easter Monday. On Christmas Day, Leigh will be met away, and on New Year's Day Runcorn away. The two latter fixtures are by an agreement played at Warrington, Leigh and Runcorn in alternate seasons. G. DICKENSON'S BENEFIT.
It has been decided to set apart the St. Helens match on October 4th as George Dickenson's benefit

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, July 5, 1913. BOWLING. WITH THE WOODS.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, July 5, 1913. BOWLING. WITH THE WOODS.
Final In Gigantic Local Handicap. --- " PETER PEACOCK" CUP.

The keen interest which is taken in bowling in Warrington was manifested to an enormous degree on Saturday, when two important local competition were concluded. The success of the " Peter Peacock " Challenge Cap Competition, promoted by the Warrington Liberal Association, has been greater than ever, and there was a large attendance of spectators to witness the final games on the beautiful green at Bank Quay. Throughout the competition a true spirit of sportsmanship and enthusiasm has pre- vailed, and each team has tried hard to win the much coveted trophy, which goes to Whitecross F, who have played most consistently all along. The committee have worked very assiduously in catering for the recreation of the ward workers, and the splendid success of the competition must be a source of satis- faction to the generous donor of the cup, Councillor Peter Peacock.

The final games in the Warrington and District handicap weie of a highly interesting character. This competition is a very popular one and is concluded in a very short time, three Saturdays sufficing for all the games. This year's winner is J. W. Monks, the popular Junior Conservative player. With a handicap of three, he has done exceedingly well in each round, and his win of 15-7 over J. Isherwood (2), Bull's Head, in the final, was well deserved. Isherwood had recorded some good wins, and in the semi-final he beat Hughes (2), Senior Conservatives, by 15-7 in 16 ends. Monks entered the final by defeating T. Humphreys (scratch), Rylands, 15-10, after 17 interesting ends. Humphreys was one of the favourites, and his defeat came as a surprise to the wireworkers. In the final Monks ran his woods in splendid fashion, and at the 7th end had an advantage of 10-3. Isherwood then recorded a double and two singles, having won only on one end previously.

Four games were played in the third round of the " Fiulayson " Cup Competition in connection with the Warrington Works Association. Howley Tannery recorded the closebt win of the day, beating Robinson's tdasswarks by two points. Bytands' No. 1 are going strong in this competition, and on Saturday they beat the Carpenters and Joiners by 15 points, winning all but tour games.

div.head: "PETER PEACOCK" CUP FINAL.
div.p: "PETER PEACOCK" CUP FINAL.

We must heartily congratulate the Whitecross F men on their splendid victory in this competition while at the same time not forgetting to commend the other teams who have played so exceptionally well all through the competition. The games on Saturday were typical examples of the high-class nature of the bowling which one witnesses in this competition. Block touchers were too numerous to count and the skill of many players was exceptional.

The green looked beautiful, and the first teams to occupy it in the fourth round were St. Austin's G (I'7) and 6t. John's B (22). The latter contingent left nothing to chance and won three games on the first four men and two on the last quartette, compiling a total of 111.

The Whitecross F men were well handicapped at 10, and in the fourth round they completely crushed the Orlord A team (28). Winning on every man, the victors gained a majority of 20 points, J. Casey and B. Jennings being the only two to record double figures.

St. Austin's F entered the semi-final by the narrow majority of one over Town Hall D, who had an advantage of five on a fifteen p int handicap. St. Austin's gained the most decisive victory of the day, for although they had to concede IS points to Fairfield G, they won by 39, never losing an individual game.

The semi-final games were intensely interesting, bu again Whitecross F had a pretty easy task, for they beat St. John's B by 36 points. W. Leigh and P. Taylor were the only Whitecross men to lose, their vanquishers being H. Langley and J. H. Seni.yr res- pectively. The St. Austin's D team thoroughly deserved their win of 15 points over St. Austin's F, for they all played exceedingly well. The final was a great game, but there is no disput- ing the fact that Whitecross were the better team. They had an advantage of three on their handicap of 16 and recorded five wins. P. Wright (captain) set a good example for Whitecross when he disposed of F. Percival by 13-10 in 15 ends. Percival had the bettor of matters at first, leading 4-2, 7-2, 9-4 and 98. Wright then led 10-9, but Percival peeled on the next end. He, however, failed to record another chalk.

W. Corlett (Whitecross) had all his work cut out to beat F. Grey by the odd chalk in 20 ends. After being in arrears 3-9 at the 10th end, Corlett secured the 'little 'un" and at the 16th end he led 11-9, only to be behind 11-12 at the 18th end. He peeled with 12 on the next end,and, running his wood well, secured the winning single.

P. Taylor (Whitecross) was getting pretty con- fident when he led 124 against .1 Griffiths after 16 ends had been played. Lfttle.did he think that that would be his final score, but such was the case, for Griffitbs astonished not only the Whitecross men, but everyone on the green, when he ran to game with six. The other games were full of exciting incidents, and all the spectators agreed that Whiteeross. win of 14 points was a true state of the games. The cup and watches were then presented to the winning team, and a full report of those proceedings, together with Mr. A. H. Crosfield's speech, appear in another column.

The semi-final game between Crosfield's and White- cross in the Consolation Competition of the Warrington and District Association was played on Saturday, and resulted in a win of 10 points, on the aggregate, for the soapery men, who played a winning game all through.

div.head: HAND-FED TROUT.
div.p: HAND-FED TROUT.

The question of the best kind of food to give to trout in waters where they are nursed and looked after is one that a good many people in the country are asking themselves at the present time. The usual thing to provide them with is butcher's refuse or horse- flesh, and it is asserted that in this carnivorous fashion they fare better and put on weight more quickly than with any other kind of nutriment. It is almost beyond dispute, however, that it has the great disadvantage of making their flesh very unpalatable. An alternative food is to be procured from Grimsby, and very possibly from other big centres of our fish supply, in the form of small sea fish for which there is no demand as human food. Really these are no more than the fry of larger fish, and it is to be regretted that they should not be allowed to remain in the sea to assist in providing our national fish food supply when they come to maturity. But since they have to be killed, incidentally on other fishing operations, it is better that they should serve as trout food than that they should be wasted, and if the trout on this cannibal diet do not put on condition so quickly as when fed on horseflesh it is certain that they are much more edible.—" Country Life."
COTTON IN AUSTRALIA. AN EXPERT WANTED.

It has for a long time been considered that Australia supplies wonderful opportunities for the cultivation of cotton, and the matter is evidently being taken up in a practical way. The Commonwealth Government ha,..? arranged to obtain the services of a cotton expert from England to adviie as to the best methods of promoting the cultivation of cotton in Australia, and is in communication with the British cotton growing association with a view of securing a suitable person for this work. The salary offered is £5OO a year. The appointment may be regarded as a direct outcome of the proceedings of the Dominions Royal Commission, as the evidence with regard to the possibilities of growing cotton of a high grade in many parts of the Commonwealth has been of a striking character, and the members of the Commission are understood to have attached considerable importance to it.

div.head: DEPLETED LEATHER STOCK.
div.p: DEPLETED LEATHER STOCK.

Messrs. S. W. Royce and Co., Manchester, in their report for June, say :-- This has been an unfortunate month in the metal markets, values showing a heavy fall all round, except in the case of lead. Prices of pig iron had been forced up too high, and gave way in alarming fashion in the closing days of May, since when there has been a further heavy decline, the total fall during the last four weeks being us. 6d. per ton in Scotch iron and 15s. 6d. per ton in Cleveland. The low prices reached, which for Cleveland iron are said to be , well below cost of production, have attracted buyers, and some fair business has been done during the last few days at improved figures. Copper has steadily fallen fully E 6 per ton, but has now recovered about £2, and is firm at present. Tin has lost £l6 during this month, or £3l since the beginning of May, and is now firmer at about £5 above the lowest. Spelter is down nearly £2 per ton, and is dull. Pig lead, after gaining 255. per ton, has eased somewhat and is now flat. THE LEATHER TRADE. INCREASE IN FOREIGN BUSINESS.

Whilst the home trade is temporarily quiet, says the "Leather World," foreign business continues to• increase and expand, and one tanner had the experi- ence last week, unique for him, of receiving in the same day buyers from the Continent, the States, and Australia. That overseas trade is advancing rapidly cannot he doubted, and leaving out of account altogether business which has been put through, but which is undelivered, the exports of leather (in the piece) for the first five months of the year are up over £200,000 on last year's figures, or, say, the entire production of four large tanyards. On the other hand, imports of foreign leather are down about an. equal amount, so that British-held stocks are getting depleted at both ends and at a rapid rate, and no argument is needed to demonstrate the position the home trade may find itself in when the "off season lassitude is over.
