div.head: WALKING DAY.
div.p: WALKING DAY.
(Continued from Page 7.)

BUCKLEY-STREET (INDEPENDENT METHODIST).— This school enjoys a reputation for origkat and picturesque pageantry, and yesterday's display was no exception to the rule. Mr. E. Taylor had acted as convener for the decorative features of the procession, and deserves great credit for his untiring efforts to make it successful. The Pioneer Brass Band headed the school, followed by the large banner representing "The Gentle Shepherd "and "The Guardian Angel." A troup of Morris dancers, admirably trained by Miss A. Whalley, executed the old-fashioned measure as they traversed the streets. Mr. E. Plinston had arranged a tableau representing the "Children of Warrington Cot" in the Infirmary, and a collection was made in aid of the funds of the institution. There was a charming little Rose Queen with maids of honour—a pleasing picture which had been designed by Miss L. Richardson. A group of fascinating fairies was in charge of Miss M. Richardson, and Quaker girls and other characters were impersonated by scholars, under the direction of Miss L. Lee. The tableau " Sunbeam," illustrating the hymn " Jesus wants me for a sunbeam " as designed by Mr. H. Woolley and Miss E. Troman. In the afternoon the children re-assembled and marched to Mr. Alcard's field in Folly- lane. Dinner and tea were served in a marquee, and the usual games were engaged in. Each , child received an orange on leaving for home. The school was originally established in Back Dallam-lane, but was transferred to the present building in 1879. Number of scholars : 212 boys ; 238 girls ; teachers, 26 ; superintendent ; Mr. A. Taylor; assistant superintendent, Mr. W. Shaw; secretary, Mr. C. F. Simpson ; assistant secretary, Mr. G. Hughes Cox.

div.head: ROMAN CATHOLIC.
div.p: ROMAN CATHOLIC.

ST. BENEDICT'S—This school had a very beautiful procession' headed by the band of St. Joseph's Industrial School, Manchester, in Gaelic costume. The handsome banners of St. Benedict, Sacred Heart, and Our Lady were displayed. Infants carried a statue of the Divine Infant, the C.Y.M.S. a statue of the Sacred Heart, and the Children of Mary a statue of Our Lady. After the procession the scholars attended Benediction in the church. In the afternoon there were tea and amusements in a field at Padgate. Established in 1836, the school has a roll of 624 scholars, with 15 teachers. The clergy taking part in the procession were the Revs. I'. 0. Swarbreck, G. C. Jackson, J. P. Wilson, T. B. McEvoy, T. Myerscough and T. Dobson. ST. ALBAN'S.—This school made a pleasing and picturesque display. The procession was headtd by the Borough Band, and the most prominent banners were those of St. Alban, Our Lady, St. Joseph, St. Agnes and the Blessed Sacrament. A statue of Our Lady was also carried. In the afternoon the children were entertained in a field at Padgate. The school was established in 1816, and has 420 scholars and 11 teachers. Clergy : Very Rev, J. P. Whittle and Rev. L. Buggins. CHURCH OF THE SACRED HEART.—The pro- cession was headed by the band of the Nautical School, Farnworth, and a pleasiog feature was the striking array of floral decorations. Decorated statues of the Sacred Heart and Our Lady were carried. The after- noon was spent in a field at Fearnhead. The schcol was established 20 years ago, and has 320 scholars and 8 teachers ; clergy, Revs. Wiliam Rockliffe and John Murphy.

ST. MARY'S (BUTTERMARKET-STREET).—This schoo maintained its high reputation for effective pageantry. Three bands were in attendance, all being associated with the League of the Cross. They were the Prize Brass Band and the bugle std drum and fife bands of the Boys' Brigade. • Two of the most beautiful banners were copies of Murillo's "Immaculate Conception " and Turner's " St. Bent diet." The seven Sacramental banners were also carried. A feature which attracted great attention was a splendid life-size, pure white statue of Our Lady, with floral structural canopy, borne by Children of Mary, and surrounded by children carrying streamers and floral wands. Four companies of the League of the Cross Boys' Brigade, attached to St. Mary's parish, made a smart show. They were under the command of Captains 'Walsh, S. J. Price, G. Dower and Lieutenant L. Cross. The bugle band was in charge of Bandmaster Martin, and the fifes were under the direction of Bandmaster Fox. The present strength of the brigade is 180. After the procession, all assembled in St. Mary's Church for Benediction. The afternoon was spent in a field at Critchley's farm' Padgate-lane. Established in 1887, the school has 800 children on ita books, with 20 teachers. The clergy taking part in the processicn were the Rev. Fathers Neville Wilson, R. Basil Primavesi and Dr. Mercer. OUR LADY'S ;LATCEIFORD).—The uniform and pretty dresses of the children were a striking feature of the procession. White suits and dresses, with crimson caps and sashes were worn, and most of the little girls carried baskets of flowers. The members of the Guild of St. Agnes had wands decorated with smilax and white lilies. The procession was headed by a cross bearer and altar boys, in cassocks and robes. Next came the band of St. Joseph's Industrial School, Stockport, followed by the following clergy: Revs. J. Tallon (rector), A. J. Wilson (assistant priest), J. H. Roche (Stockport), Geo. Conroy (Birkenhead), and the Very Rev. Canon Chambers (Chester). A very handsome banner of Our Lady was followed uy the boys of the day and Sunday school, Guild of St. Aloyseus, Children of Mary (with statue of Our Lady), gills of day and Sunday school (Guild of St. Agnes) and Young Men's Society. After the procession, all returned to church for Benediction, the singing of the children's choir being very impressive. In the afternoon there was the usual field sports, for which prizes were given.

div.head: UNDENOMINATIONAL.
div.p: UNDENOMINATIONAL.

RAGGED SCHOOL-11e scholars. numbering 400, met at 8.30 and, haying been presented with cakes, marched to the park and joined the procession round the town. Returning to the school,they were conveyed on lurries, kindly lent by Lady Greenell, to the park at Grappenhall Hayes. generously placed at the disposal of the school by Mr. J.Charlton Parr. Dinner and tea were served and games engaged in. The school was estab- lished in 1887 and is undenominational. Councillor .1. Skelland is the founder and superintendent.
Photograph by Burrell. ASCENDING FOR THE FIRST RIDE. • The Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth, Alderman Bennett ,and Alderman Smethurst.

Two of the motor 'buses which the Corporation is providing to link up the tramway services arrived this week and were first used on Thursday. Alder- man Smethurst (chairman if the Tramways Com- mittee) aid other members of the Council made a trial trip in the morning, and since then the new buses have been remarkably well patronised. They start from Market Gate, one going to Gorsey-lane and the other being used for a circular tour to Lovely- lane and round the Bewsey district, the fare for each round being one penny. The vehicles are handsome in appearance, run smoothly, and almost noiselessly. The rubber band tyres are the product of a local firm—the St. Helens Cable and Rubber Co., Ltd. We understand that they are a distinct improvement upon any tyres of the kind, being made under a patent of the works manager, Mr. E. S Seymour. The principal point in manufacture, which is quite distinct from that if any other type, is to embody a specially rekilient rubber underneath the tread rubber, so that the Shocks of the road are taken up, which thus reduces the vibration and also reduces the wear upon the tread. These tyres are running upon other ‘tiarlington ccmn:lercial cars, and have proved all the qualities claimed for them.

THE SPHINX IN THEBES (MASS.) There was a woman in a steel-ibuilt city who had all that money buys; she had gold and divi- dends and trains and houses; and she had pets to play with—dogs, monkeys, and parakeets; only she had no sphinx. So she besought . them to bring her a live sphinx, and therefore they went to the mena- geries, and then to the forests and the desert places, and yet could find no sphinx: And she would have been content with a little lion, but 'that one was already owned by a woman she knew; so they had to search the world again for a sphinx. And still there was none. But they were not men that it is easy to baffle, and at last they found a sphinx in a deseiit at evening watching a ruined temple whose gods she had eaten hundreds of years ago when her hunger was on her. And they cast chains' on her, who was still with an ominous silence, and took her back with them and brought her home. And so the sphinx came to the steel-built city. And the woman was very glad that she owned a sphinx. But the sphinx asked a riddle of the woman, and stared long into her eyes, and said: "What is the value, in dollars, of a soul?" And the woman could not answer, and she died. And the sphinx is silent again, and none knows what she will do.- I',RD DUNBANY in Saturday neriew.
